Bipartite graphs illustrate the connections between two non-overlapping groups of entities and are frequently depicted with a two-level arrangement. In this representation, each group occupies a parallel horizontal row, containing vertices, and directed edges link the rows. A common objective in these visualizations is to reduce the number of edge intersections, ideally achieving a minimal crossing number. Because finding an optimal solution often requires a vast search space, metaheuristic approaches are typically employed. This study introduces a novel framework that transforms these problems into a continuous optimization task using a newly devised cost function. This method formulates the minimum crossing number as a loss function within a continuous framework, where variables include both vertex and position parameters. By integrating this approach with Population-Based Training (PBT), the authors demonstrate that the method successfully minimizes crossings in benchmark instances. Furthermore, the study illustrates how this technique can be applied to optimize intersections when embedding edges of planar 1-plane bipartite graphs.

Deep learning models typically require extensive, balanced data for training, a condition rarely met in real-world applications, especially in Incremental Learning (IL), where new data streams are continuous and often skewed toward certain classes. This category imbalance frequently induces negative transfer and pseudo-overfitting, phenomena wherein the model disproportionately prioritizes recently added classes at the expense of older ones. To mitigate these issues without the constraints of a balanced dataset, we introduce a Confidence-Agnostic Contrastive Learning (CACL) framework for IL that enhances deep features through confidence-agnostic contrastive optimization. Concurrently, to reinforce memory for old concepts, the method integrates Mutual Information Maximization (MIM) to secure high-quality prototypes representing former classes. Experiments across three continuous IL benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces a new concept in bipedal robotics known as hybrid dynamics, which integrates orbital mechanics with impact theory to describe the complete walking cycle. Our proposed model combines continuous dynamics driven by thrusters for mid-flight adjustments with instantaneous impact dynamics occurring at foot contact. By unifying these continuous and discrete phases, we achieve a comprehensive mathematical framework for walking. This model facilitates the direct formulation of control objectives and allows for the application of advanced control strategies, including Model Predictive Control (MPC) and feedback linearization. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by presenting the design of a MPC controller within this new model. Simulation results confirm the method, showing successful stabilization of a complex 4-degree-of-freedom walking pattern on a test case.

Building upon the work of Denef and Loeser, this paper establishes a version of their motivivic Milnor long exact sequence applicable to equations of the form $f(\bar{x})=g(\bar{x})-\gamma$ within certain Henselian valued fields possessing a linear form, where both $f$ and $g$ are either polynomials or rational functions. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the global motivivic Milnor one-cocycle decomposes into the sum of individual local cocycles computed over residue maps; specifically, these local components are proven to be surjective in the described restricted fields classes. Consequently, an exact sequence for the motivivic Milnor one-cocycles is derived as a direct corollary. In an additional contribution, a version of the change of variables theorem for the global motivivic Milnor one-cocycle formula is presented, with all coefficients in the associated motivivic integration change of variables sequence explicitly calculated.

Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial precursor for side-channel attacks, enabling them to overcome specific barriers. This paper introduces a novel technique that exploits Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT) architectures to further refine such methods, thereby expanding the scope of potential targets. The proposed approach ensures that multiple threads within an SMT environment experience controlled, distinct slowdowns. By decoupling the clock frequencies of different architectural components and adjusting the scheduling of instructions across threads, the implementation achieves selective performance degradation. The authors present "ClockSeparate," a solution that separates system clock frequencies into a core clock and multiple thread clocks. Experimental results indicate that this method is highly effective in SMT environments, generating a per-thread frequency approximately 1.4 times lower than the nominal system rate while operating at only 140% of the core frequency. Furthermore, the research demonstrates the practical application of this mechanism to the first-ever side-channel attack on a Software Defined Radio (SDR) system specifically running in TLM (Thread Local Memory) mode.

We examine the possibility of the $g-2$ anomaly being explained by resonant enhancements of the Higgs boson coupling to either bottom quarks ($b$) or tau leptons ($\tau$), provided the resonance is otherwise decoupled from Standard Model (SM) particles. In both scenarios, the required explanation for the anomaly involves a resonance mass near 1 TeV. However, these interactions inevitably produce detectable signatures in various Higgs boson decay channels; notably, the scenario invoking tau couplings generates significant enhancements in the di-Higgs final state. Furthermore, the 1 TeV resonance explanation for the $g-2$ anomaly is increasingly disfavored by recent data from the LHCb detector regarding dilepton resonances and ATLAS data concerning diphoton resonances.

This document presents LHCb's methodology for accurately determining the CKM angle $\phi$ (or angle eta) using time-dependent $B$-meson ($B^0$) oscillations. It focuses on the decay of the particle into the CP eigenstate $K^+ K^-$ via the process $B^0 \to K^+ K^-$, governed by the CKM matrix element $V_{ts}^*$. This level of accuracy is critical for identifying rare decays and improving the overall understanding of the Standard Model. The procedure employs advanced statistical techniques, including maximum likelihood estimation, to incorporate additional constraints from global CKM fits and improve the reliability of the result. By leveraging large datasets and high-resolution timing resolution, LHCb provides a robust contribution to the global effort in characterizing the CKM matrix.

Federized learning maintains model privacy by distributing data across multiple parties. It is broadly categorized into horizontal and vertical setups based on how that data is spread. In horizontal federated learning, each participant holds distinct datasets, whereas vertical federated learning assumes every party shares a common identifier key along with specific auxiliary attributes attached to those records. This article introduces a novel horizontal-to-vertical federated learning transformation that adapts a vertical solution to function as horizontal one simply by reassigning data partitions. We further examine the conditions required to replicate the accuracy of an existing horizontal model using their vertical counterpart using this new approach.

Kernel methods constitute a potent tool for addressing numerous machine learning challenges, particularly in optimization and regression tasks. However, their reliance on pairwise operations causes computational complexity to expand proportionally with dataset size, restricting their applicability to large data environments. Although various acceleration techniques have been proposed, they often introduce difficulties regarding theoretical guarantees or practical implementation. This paper introduces Randomized Low-Rank Kernel Approximation (RLRKA), a streamlined framework that delivers reliable estimates for both functional outputs and target values. The RLRKA approach first generates a low-rank positive semi-definite matrix close to the true kernel matrix and subsequently supplies a stochastically rounded label for each datapoint. We demonstrate that RLRKA yields a rapidly computable solution, which, when combined with standard stochastic gradient descent, guarantees parameter estimates within an $\epsilon$ error margin with high probability. Furthermore, the method provides rigorous bounds estimating both prediction error and regression deviation. Empirical evaluations across various large-scale benchmarks indicate that RLRKA outperforms existing state-of-the-art kernel algorithms in both speed and accuracy.

Determining the optimal timing for pulmonary valve replacement in Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients is vital for minimizing adverse outcomes and reducing healthcare costs. Because this decision-making problem involves multiple conflicting objectives, traditional methods often fall short. This study introduces a Multiobjective Net Benefit (MNB) approach, utilizing it to identify an ideal range for valve replacement timing that balances key metrics. We evaluated our method using a TOF patient cohort from the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, incorporating objective data on right ventricular size, right ventricular function, and left-to-right shunt fraction to form our multiobjective framework. Results demonstrate that the solution space is not singular; rather, an infinite set of equally optimal solutions exists. This confirms the MNB method's efficacy in offering a decision-support mechanism for clinicians managing TOF patients.

We establish the Gamma-convergence of these continuous functionals to a counterpart proposed by Amritah and Braides, which replaces the coherent interfacial term with an anisotropic, metric-based surface energy. Additionally, we introduce and analytically support a novel class of discretized variational schemes. The convergence of this grid formulation is proven via the Gamma-convergence to the limit functional derived by Amritah and Braides, thus providing a valid numerical method for handling these therapeutically significant strong singular perturbations.

This work examines an optimal scheduling challenge in a multi-user mobile data networks framework incorporating Simultaneous Wireless Information and Power Transfer (SWIPT). The study focuses on a time-slotted system where base station serves multiple source and drain users per interval. The scheduling goal is to maximize the total interval count over a finite horizon, accounting for both information reception and power harvesting. The paper establishes the time-sharing optimality of a novel alternating greedy algorithm, referred to as TAG. Furthermore, it introduces an power-up alternating greedy approach, named PTAG, which enhances performance by boosting power supply to sinks without incurring additional algorithmic overhead or sacrificing performance, based on power supply augmentation. The work further derives performance bounds for both algorithms. Simulation outcomes highlight the effectiveness of the proposed strategies.

The Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) has significantly advanced object detection, yet it occasionally produces false positives for large-scale objects. In the case of such false detections, the initial convolutional layers extract discriminative features, but the bottom-up high-resolution low-level outputs upsampled to a large scale result in poor object detail. Addressing this, we propose a new FPN architecture that replaces the standard upsampled low-level features with mid-level features, which already possess a resolution matching the target high resolution. Experiments across COCO and Visual Genome datasets confirm that this method reduces false detections of large objects while maintaining or improving performance on other categories, with the improvement in large-object detection specifically attributed to a higher Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold of 0.6.

In this work, we address the problem of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD), which involves identifying the appropriate meaning for a target word within a specific sentence context. Since some words possess multiple senses, their surface text can appear misleading without considering their usage environment. To illustrate, the word "bank" functions differently depending on whether the context is "I went to the bank to withdraw some money" (referring to an institution) or "Go to the left bank to avoid the curve" (referring to an outdoor slope). Given that each word sense carries a unique definition, we propose a new WSD framework built on context-based meaning extraction using a BERT-based approach combined with a contrastive learning strategy. Our system operates in two stages: initially, it identifies all potential word senses and generates a contextualized meaning vector for each; subsequently, it selects the correct sense by identifying the closest match to the original word sense embeddings using a cosine similarity metric. Experiments were conducted on two standard WSD datasets to validate our approach. Our results indicate that our model outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating higher accuracy in these evaluations.

Comprehending and carrying out everyday activities often requires interpreting multiple modalities of communication, such as spoken and written language, visuals, and sensory feedback. To understand and execute these real-world procedures, competent communication across these diverse modalities is essential.

Addressing network vulnerabilities is crucial for understanding complex systems. This paper introduces a novel, attack-resilient network metric based on a new concept: the "network avalanche." By analyzing an attack model where a network is stressed by sequentially eliminating its largest-degree node, we investigate what happens when a tie exists for the maximum degree. We define the avalanche as the count of nodes eliminated during a single attack step under such tie conditions. To study networks immediately prior to a potential avalanche, we derive and solve equations that calculate a probability measure known as the post-avalanche weight. Utilizing these tools, we develop a methodology to quantify the likelihood of an avalanche event in various network states and apply these findings to three specific models: Erdős–Rényi random graphs, scale-free Barabási–Albert networks, and small-world Watts–Strogatz topologies. Our analysis reveals that avalescences appear with high frequency in both random and typical scale-free architectures but remain rare in small-world networks. Understanding avalanche dynamics and the resulting metric offers significant insights into network structure and enhances our comprehension of attack mechanisms and resilience.

This work examines the properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials defined on $\mathbb{R}^+$ with respect to the generalised Airy weight $x^{(\beta+\omega)}\mathrm{e}^{-x^{\alpha/3}}\theta(x)$, where $\alpha, \beta, \omega \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\alpha \in (0,2)$. In addressing these properties, we specifically investigate the asymptotic behaviour of the corresponding $n$th-order polynomial $P_{n}(z)$ as $n \to \infty$. This asymptotic analysis relies crucially on the asymptotic distribution of zeros for an associated algebraic equation, a problem resolved via the application of Tricomi's Truncated Hilbert Transform technique.

Ambient electromagnetic radiation is frequently overlooked as a source of high-frequency noise in gravitational-wave detectors; however, we demonstrate that at frequencies exceeding 1 kHz, this background is orders of magnitude more intense than the photon-shot noise typically defining the sensitivity floor of photon-counting setups. Consequently, this electromagnetic noise sets a fundamental ceiling for the achievable sensitivity of such detectors. To mitigate the issue, we evaluate various noise-reduction strategies, including active suppression, physical shielding, and opto-mechanical designs that circumvent the limitation, ultimately projecting the potential sensitivity gains attainable by addressing this high-frequency limit.

Extra-large MIMO (XL-MIMO) systems, featuring widely spaced antenna elements, offer significant advantages in dense user environments. However, these systems are highly susceptible to antenna element mismatches, leading to visible spatial beam patterns that can cause major fairness issues in the allocation of resources. This paper introduces a novel fairness-centric framework for resource allocation in XL-MIMO networks, incorporating a closed-form solution to maximize the minimum spectral efficiency while keeping user data rates in mind. Building on this foundation, a low-complexity, data-driven algorithm is proposed to optimize sum spectral efficiency by intelligently grouping users. Simulation outcomes indicate that these approaches deliver superior performance compared to existing methods.

High angular resolution observations reveal that disks surrounding infant stars frequently exhibit dynamic behavior, often characterized by spiral features, warps, and clumps. Theoretical models indicate that such structures arise from gravitational interactions within the disks, specifically through the formation of spiral arms triggered by embedded planetary bodies. Although numerous observations have provided strong evidence for the presence of planets within these systems, the direct detection of free-floating sub-Jovian planets in protoplanetary environments remains elusive. To address this, we utilized the ALMA observatory to conduct deep, sensitive imaging at high spatial resolution for the disk associated with the T Tauri star SU Aur, an system previously noted for its intricate structure. Our findings confirm that SU Aur's disk structure is highly complex, with spiral patterns detected across all observed spatial scales. Furthermore, assuming the surface brightness distribution adheres to an $m=3$ spiral density wave model, our analysis yields robust constraints on the position and mass of any potential self-gravitating planet responsible for these disturbances.

The nature of the second compact object involved in the GW190814 event—specifically whether it is a stellar-mass black hole or a neutron star—has been a subject of recent debate. In this study, we examine the possibility that an equation of state (EOS) exists capable of producing a maximum neutron star mass matching the value reported in GW190814. We utilized the relativistic EOS formalism for symmetric nuclear matter, incorporating correlations and fluctuations to determine EOSs under uncertain conditions. Our results indicate that even with these stochastic effects, it is feasible to generate a maximum neutron star mass of 2.60 $M_{\odot}$, a finding that supports the interpretation of the GW190814 secondary as a neutron star. Additionally, we analyzed the tidal deformability of neutron stars with this 2.60 $M_{\odot}$ maximum mass in light of tidal-wave constraints derived from the neutron star-black hole merger event GW190812.

Furthermore, incorporating spin–orbit coupling yields a minor band gap of 0.15 eV, confirming SrMnO$_3$ as a narrow-bandgap semiconductor. The work also analyzes the origins of this splitting and evaluates its impact on SrMnO$_3$'s overall electronic characteristics.

Using first-principles calculations, we evaluated the total energies of various local structural motifs within BaTiO$_3$ in its paraelectric phase. We identify that simple cubic arrangements of TiO$_6$ octahedra—specifically the fully oxygenated perovskite structure (PC) and related superlattice variants like the $3\times3\times3$ supercell—exhibit markedly higher stability. In contrast, non-coordinated configurations, defined by empty spaces between these TiO$_6$ octahedra, lie significantly higher in energy. Consequently, fully oxygenated perovskites emerge as the most essential structural building blocks for modeling the structural, dielectric, and ferroelectric characteristics of BaTiO$_3$ and likely many related perovskites. Furthermore, our analysis of electronic and elastic properties for these structural types supports the conclusion that structural distortions in BaTiO$_3$ are driven by orbital ordering.

Recently, the electronic structure of graphene has been recognized as consisting of two layers: an outer band of Dirac electrons formed by carbon atoms in a honeycomb lattice, and an inner band comprising non-Dirac electrons generated by hybridization with hydrogen adsorption. We demonstrate that a triangular optical lattice, imprinted on this bimodal graphene system, supports a diverse array of strong interaction-driven phenomena. By analyzing the effective Hamiltonian and its corresponding matrix structure, we identify that such bimodal systems on a optical lattice yield a set of coupled models. These include a Hund's-coupled multi-orbital system, a multi-orbital ferromagnetic system, and a multi-orbital Hund's antiferromagnetic variant. Furthermore, we investigate the system's phase diagram and reveal the coexistence of multiple phases, specifically highlighting a CO-REPPING state paired with a repulsive Hund's antiferromagnetic phase. Finally, we calculate the Green's functions and spectral functions to illustrate how these emerging interaction-induced phases manifest within the energy bands.

The beta distribution, commonly utilized for continuous data confined to the unit interval, suffers from an inability to model natural breaks or gaps, a significant limitation given that many datasets within such bounds possess these features. Although various beta-mixture alternatives exist to address gap creation, they frequently yield complex structures that hinder analytical work and visualization. This paper introduces the truncated beta distribution, a distributional alternative tailored specifically for data gaps on the unit interval, while maintaining simplicity and providing a closed-form solution. We derive its characteristics, construct acceptance-rejection sampling methods, and present empirical results demonstrating its practical utility.

"We discuss the spectral shift observed in the spectral gyroscopic Saagnac interferometer, attributing it to the change in effective cavity length within a rotating Gyrator integrated into the Sagnac loop. This shift arises because the gyrator alters the cavity's physical dimensions relative to light propagation during rotation, generating a frequency change independent of any cumulative phase or path difference between clockwise and counter-clockwise directions. This phenomenon offers a novel approach to producing large spectral shifts that fit into a compact device, enabling the spectral gyroscopic Sagnic effect to function as a compact, high-sensitivity rotation detector capable of generating shifts significantly larger than typical ones found in standard fiber configurations."

This paper continues the investigation initiated in Part I regarding the theory of real algebraic groups and their actions, specifically addressing coactions on varieties. A subset $S \subset V$ qualifies as a Weierstrass submanifold if, for each $v \in V$, there exists an $s \in S$ such that the orbit through $s$ dominates every other such orbit in the partial ordering induced by the action's algebraic structure (i.e., $\dim G\cdot s \leq \dim G\cdot v$ for all $v$). Under specific conditions, it is demonstrated that Weberstrass submanifolds exist within any given regular orbit and are uniquely determined when $V$ is compact. Furthermore, a strong connection is established between the order of roots of a regular root system and these submanifolds. The paper concludes by considering regular root systems of type $F$ and describing the corresponding order on the associated roots.

Although neural language models (LMs) have largely superseded traditional $N$-gram models due to their higher performance, the neural approach incurs significantly greater costs. This research explores ways to enhance the capabilities of $N$-gram models despite these high costs. We introduce a method that captures the knowledge of a pre-trained neural LM by constructing a discrete, finite-state approximation. This is achieved by deriving a finite automaton that accepts strings scoring proportionally to the perplexity of the target neural model. We evaluate this approach against a baseline factorized $N$-gram system using the Wikipedia corpus, testing two widely adopted neural models: the average-encoding baseline and the attention-based model introduced in [1]. Results indicate that our improved model outperforms the factorized baseline by a mean of 1.33 bits per character across both neural references, suggesting that the enhanced approximation effectively retrieves knowledge from the pretrained neural models. Consequently, this improved $N$-gram framework can be deployed at minimal computational cost while retaining a substantial portion of the original performance.

Accurately reconstructing and aligning faces in 3D from images remains a challenging task, particularly when dealing with occlusions and diverse head poses, for which existing 3D tools often falter. This paper introduces a new methodology for dense 3D face alignment and modeling that effectively handles occluded and head-displaced scenarios. The core innovation is a dual system: a target-oriented one trained on clean images and a source-oriented one, also trained on pristine data but designed to work within the influence of alternative alignments produced by other algorithms. To bridge the gap between these alternatives, we provide a geometric correction technique that adjusts a source model using a reference alignment generated by an external method—such as a 2D face detector or an alternative 3D aligner—thereby reducing modeling discrepancies. The synergy between the dual systems enables robust 98% accuracy on the 3D Alignment and Verification Challenge dataset, significantly improving performance for faces that are occluded or positioned away from the center.

We investigate the simultaneous breaking of spatial translation and gauge symmetries within Witten's cubic model to establish a unified framework for fractonic quantum phases. This approach enables the description of various well-known fractonic models, including the subsector-based fractonic phases characterized by symmetric, broken symmetric, $U(1)$, and $SU(2)$ gauge theories, as well as the complex Haah's cube model. In our analysis, various fractonic excitations are categorized by type based on whether they propagate diagonally, along single directions, or not at all, demonstrating how to interconnect these categories through model intertwinement. We further explore phase transitions and the application of our methods to the study of monopole formation in dipolar gauge theories.

Utilizing an axion-like particle (ALP) model coupled with an ALP decay mode, we investigate the cosmological genesis of primordial black holes (PBHs) within high-density early-universe environments. We establish that significant halos or clusters of PBHs can emerge if the ALP self-coupling $\lambda$ is negative and sufficiently large in magnitude, specifically within the range of $-150 < \lambda < -50$. This formation mechanism relies on the expansion of the universe following reheating, occurring when $\lambda$ is moderately negative and the AlP mass $m_a$ is small. In this scenario, Hubble friction suppresses AlP oscillations, allowing coherent field fluctuations to grow into large local energy densities upon decaying into AlP particles. Our analysis further demonstrates that this ALP-induced formation channel can account for the observed dark matter density through appropriate choices of $m_a$ and $\lambda$. Additionally, this framework generates substantial out-of-equilibrium AlP populations post-rehearing, generating distinctive signatures in high-energy AlP physics experiments.

This paper addresses the analysis of marked ordered trees, a class where each node is tagged with a symbol from a finite alphabet, with tree validity determined by unique symbol occurrences on only node-disjoint paths from root to deepest level. The study examines the count of " Deepest" nodes—those at maximum depth—in such trees when nodes number $n$, utilizing analytic combinatorics. As $n$ grows, these deepest nodes converge in distribution to a Poisson process on the interval $[0,1]$, allowing the derivation of limit laws for various functionals of the deepest nodes vector. Specifically, for large $n$ in trees with $n$ total nodes, the average number of deepest nodes approaches **1**, while the variance tends toward **1**.

This investigation seeks to assess the capabilities of Inte**lligently** **OCR (iOCR)**. Developed to rectify inaccuracies common in standard OCR systems during vote count**s**, **iOCR** incorporates a corrective algorithm for spell checks. **The study reveals that iOCR proves superior to conventional methods.**

Recent research has examined the application of machine learning within econometrics, prioritizing methodologies grounded in rigorous theoretical frameworks. This paper presents a penalized likelihood approach for high-dimensional linear regression problems contaminated with outliers, utilizing an $l_1$-penalty to induce sparsity. Under specific conditions of outlyingness, we establish consistency for estimated parameters and determine sparsity patterns. We also derive non-asymptotic bounds for both total risk and false discovery rate. Our results indicate that, assuming independent and identically distributed data, these risks converge at a rate slower by a factor of $\sqrt{\log p}$ relative to standard outlier-free scenarios involving memory processes. Furthermore, incorporating a long-memory structure into the data can accelerate convergence, potentially improving the false discovery rate outcome by a factor of $m^{-\delta}$, where $m$ denotes the mixing coefficient's scope.

Speech enhancement serves as a vital pillar for other significant audio technologies, including speech recognition and synthesis, holding major importance in the field. This study introduces a new deep learning framework for this task, which implements a total phase spectrum loss function. By decomposing the total phase into smooth and detailed phase components, the proposed method reconstructs the target detail phase via learning, thereby enhancing accuracy. Experiments indicate that this approach not only surpasses existing techniques under evaluations involving normalized cross-correlation, mean squared error, and weighted ERB-filtered spectrum distance but also delivers superior outcomes in speech synthesis and automatic speech recognition.

By sustaining an internal pressure lower than the external environment, these spaces prevent contaminated aerosols from escaping to adjacent areas. This research introduces a novel predictive model for Negative Pressure Rooms (NPRs) utilizing Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). Storage units in electrical networks are critical for maintaining system security and maximizing economic outcomes. This study examines storage units with risk-averse attitudes facing stochastic electricity price volatility. These resources optimize a trade-off between expected profit and risk exposure, utilizing various Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) formulations. The analysis investigates how such units influence electricity prices and volatility, observing that they act as price stabilizers by purchasing power during high-cost periods and reducing supply at high prices. Additionally, the study highlights that a storage unit's aversion to risk significantly impacts both price movements and volatility patterns.

Within quantum systems, the evolution of superposition states between electronic configurations occurs on ultrafast timescales, prompting the need for an accurate theoretical framework capable of describing and predicting electron dynamics within the attosecond domain. While such predictions rely on solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, the validity of this approach is contingent upon verifying that the underlying one-particle image representation remains valid on these extreme timescales. To this end, we employ tomographic imaging of electron density using attosecond-duration soft x-ray pulses spanning a range of photon energies. Our analysis suggests this novel technique can achieve temporal resolutions better than one attosecond and possess sufficient density sensitivity to validate whether the single-particle picture holds. Specifically, we utilize molecular jet beams, where the presence of multiple nuclei enables the detection of nuclear- and electron-induced oscillations in the molecular XANES spectra, thereby providing a direct measure of temporal precision. Furthermore, the distinct variations of these oscillations across different photon energies allow for the unambiguous separation of electronic and nuclear contributions to the signal.

We investigated the General Circulation of an Earth-like atmosphere within the context of a simplified, two-dimensional, general-circulation model. Our model incorporates an Earth-scale baroclinic atmosphere, where the primary zonally symmetric baroclinic instability serves to trigger the development of distinct zonal jets. We found that a planet's rotation rate critically determines the formation and stability mechanisms of these jets. Specifically, under slow-rotating, Earth-scale conditions, barotropic and baroclinical instabilities are required to sustain the first jet, whereas a globally uniform, Earth-scale atmosphere driven solely by the primary baroclinic instability can sustain multiple, long-wavelength jets during faster rotation. We also examined how varying the latitudinal gradient of thermal forcing influences the formation of the equatorial jet. Our simulations indicate that a strong thermal forcing gradient promotes a stable equatorial jet through an enhanced, first-mode baroclinic instability during the inter-jet interval interval. Conversely, this equatorial jet disappears when the thermal forcing is uniform across latitudes or when the forcing gradient is weak.

Active learning (AL) seeks to identify the most informative data samples for labeling, while self-supervised pretraining (SSL) enables the generation of initial knowledge from unlabeled inputs to accelerate the convergence of a decoder model. Although AL and SSL address different challenges, they can be seen as complementary; therefore, this study explores integrating them to enhance the efficiency of data utilization and reduce dependency on expensive annotations. Our strategy involves two primary stages. In the first stage, we apply SSL to generate pretraining weights for the supervised component using a vast collection of unlabeled data. Subsequently, we focus our annotation resources on a smaller subset of informative samples selected via active learning. Experimental results indicate that our approach achieves a significant performance boost, delivering a 3% improvement in F1-score relative to baseline active learning methods.

This paper explores fresh perspectives on generalized algebraic multiplexing, potentially through novel approaches rooted in Algebraic Geometry where this multiplex can be localized and expressed as a local intersection index between algebra varieties. These discoveries include discovering new formulas for computing the multiplex, particularly for nilpotent elements within the local algebra $A/\mathfrak{m}$. Demonstration via illustrative cases in dimensions 2 and 3 highlights their application and effectiveness.

We introduce a proposal to simulate bosonic pair production utilizing an ensemble of long-lived atoms coupled to a high-quality cavity. This setup enables inter-atomic interaction mediated by virtual photons, specifically describing the phenomenon where entanglement between atoms increases rapidly as two-level systems approach an effective infinite potential well. To implement this simulation, we introduce a novel entanglement-based verification method suitable for scenarios involving large-dimensional quantum systems. Furthermore, based on practical inter-atomic parameters, we outline a viable experimental framework within a superconducting circuit architecture.

Donor spins in silicon have established themselves as a promising model system for quantum computing, with ongoing research focused on engineering two-phosphorus (2P) donor states to optimize their coupling and interactions. This work employs an exact numerical method to investigate the dynamics of two correlated donor electrons, exploring their response to single- and two-quantum ($\sigma^-$ to $0$ or $\sigma^+$) microwave pulses. The study concentrates on parameter regimes where the donor spacing is small, resulting in strong exchange interactions and overlapping electron wave functions. We identify distinct operational regimes characterized by unique spin dynamics and non-classical correlations between donors. Specifically, we analyze pathways for coherent control of states with anti-node valley coherence—where valley superpositions prevent destructive interference—and "valley locked" states—where exchange coupling dictates a single valley component. In both scenarios, the donor positions induce characteristic patterns in the donor-averaged electron density and modulation of the exchange coupling, which can be probed optically via donor luminescence. These signature features offer a potential means to optically read out the joint valley and charge states of the donors.

We present measurements of negative magnetoresistance in HgTe quantum wells that host a 2D topological insulator, a phenomenon marked by helical edge states emerging under an applied magnetic field. This associated negative magnetoresistance is attributed to the interference between electron paths traveling through distinct spatial regions of the device. The effect is amplified by the presence of a perpendicular in-plane field, which facilitates the creation of Landau levels and correlates directly with the development of the 2D topological insulator status. The provided model successfully accounts for the observed negative magnetoresistance, offering insight into interference patterns across sample boundaries and defining a method to characterize the formation of 2D topological insulators in HgTe quantum wells via this signature effect.

UAVs have become increasingly popular for a wide range of applications, and this study proposes an intersection management system utilizing unmanned aerial vehicles to control traffic at road junctions. A specific focus is placed on an integrated protocol combining terrestrial and vehicular communications. Within the described framework, intersections are monitored by a designated "supervisor" node, which exchanges data with nearby vehicles through short-range, high-speed wireless technology. Simultaneously, these vehicles maintain contact with the node through a long-range connection. If a supervisor detects an impending traffic accident based on data from its environment sensor, it alerts concerned vehicles via the wireless protocol. The primary objective of this research involves determining the optimal positioning for supervisor nodes to maximize coverage, as this area is contingent upon the density of traffic participants. This paper derives the localization of such coverage-maximizing optimal hotspots as a function of the density of vehicles. It further investigates optimal placement strategies assuming vehicle nodes are randomly distributed according to the homogeneous Poisson point process model. The theoretical findings are substantiated by numerical simulations to confirm their practical validity.

Dynamic time-division duplexing (TDD) allows each base station to adapt its scheduling independently, adapting upload and download rates per antenna pair based on current traffic. However, this flexibility creates radio interference, as neighboring nodes might differ in their download/upload division. This research investigates the impact of dynamic TDD on both throughput and latency in cellular networks. It introduces a new traffic model capturing realistic web-download and -upload latencies, moving beyond simplified mean values. To address these objectives, it proposes two novel resource allocation algorithms: a throughput-maximizing method utilizing a greedy approach, and a latency-minimizing algorithm employing a sophisticated queue-length policy. Simulations using Google data for traffic patterns demonstrate that these schemes substantially outperform existing solutions, delivering more than a tenfold increase in throughput and latency improvements exceeding a factor of 50.

Despite over four decades of study, the origin of the Hall anomaly in the voltage-current characteristics of granular type-II superconductors remains unresolved. In this work, we propose that this anomaly arises from the Hall resistivity progressions observed in vortex lattice systems exhibiting significant vacuume dynamics. By employing a parallel interpolation technique, we converted the three-dimensional voltage-current data of a Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8 delta vortex island into a two-dimensional dataset representing a single vortex line scan across a material plane. This adapted data was subsequently compared against three-dimensional voltage data acquired from a bi2Sr2CaCu2O8 delta vortex line during perpendicular movement across a bi3Sr3CaCu2O12 superlattice. The results indicate a qualitative match between the vacuum fluctuations associated with bi2Sr2CaCu2O8 delta vortex lattice and the vacuum fluctuations observed in the bi2Sr2CaCu2O8 delta vortex island measurement, leading us to attribute the Hall anomaly in type-II superconducting films to phenomena occurring at the vortex line scale. This finding suggests that the Hall anomaly serves as an effective signature for strong vacuume lattice melting within vortex systems.

This study analyzes critical dynamics within heavy-ion collisions, specifically focusing on the correlation between the order parameter and the control parameter near a second-order phase transition. The analysis is grounded in the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau (TDGL) framework, utilizing a coupling term proportional to the order parameter times the control parameter. By identifying the fixed point and critical exponents in both the fixed-point values and the evolution towards or away from that point—undergoing a phase transition from disorder to order—we observe a distinctive symmetry. Specifically, the distribution of time spent in specific states near the transition exhibits a "time spent" symmetry: the duration required to reach the order state from the disordered side mirrors the duration needed to return to the initial state, effectively acting as a reversible transition despite the underlying dissipative dynamics. This symmetry holds regardless of whether the system transitions from disorder to order or vice versa, with the time spent in each state being equal. This finding is notable because it occurs even within a dissipative context described by TDGL equations, with the duration of time in one state matching the duration in the opposite state exactly, appearing uniquely in this dissip framework.

We characterize finite-dimensional commuting squares of $C^*$-algebras possessing a unique faithful tracial state, applying these findings specifically to the case of hyperfinite $II_1$ subfactor pairs with matching indices.

This study introduces a meta-learning algorithm utilizing ODE-based neural networks that explicitly learn gradient relationships. By equipping optimizers with learned gradients, this method introduces a flexible architecture, particularly advantageous when combined with meta-learning strategies. Experiments demonstrate its capacity to accelerate convergence across a range of tasks, including mini-batch image classification on ImageNet, basic regression problems, and refining gradient estimates from noisy zeroth-order or first-order data. Comparisons with leading optimization benchmarks and neural network models confirm these findings. A core contribution of our work is a rigorous theoretical analysis proving that gradient function approximations converge to true gradients under broad conditions, with our data indicating this approach is well-suited for driving end-to-end optimization processes.

Enhanced model accuracy alone is insufficient; building trustworthy AI is equally vital for creating resilient systems in high-stakes fields like healthcare, finance, and autonomous vehicles, where decisions directly impact human safety. Such applications must address diverse challenges, including data and distribution shifts, adversarial attacks, privacy concerns, and various attack vectors. To navigate these issues, we present a review of recent advancements in robustness, covering attacks and defenses, evaluation metrics, and potential future research avenues.

Detecting prohibited objects in X-ray imaging is vital for public safety and remains a significant challenge due to low contrast, complex backgrounds, and object overlap. To address these issues, we introduce a Dual-Head Attention Network (DHAN) optimized for DHAN for DHAN (DHAN) (DHAN). We introduce the Prohibited Object Detection (POD) framework. This model incorporates a Lateral Inhibition Module (LIM) to enhance the separation of overlapping objects and a new POD loss function designed to improve bounding box precision. Experiments on the X-ray Prohibited Objects (X-ray Prohibited Objects) dataset demonstrate that our method surpasses existing approaches, achieving a 5.4% improvement in mAP scores over the YOLOv3 baseline. We introduce $J_n^T$, a new polynomial invariant defined specifically for the figure-eight knot known as the $n$th toroidal colored Jones polynomial. This object functions as an approximation of the standard colored Jones polynomial. Our research establishes that $J_n^T$ maintains core properties found in the original polynomial, notably a Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev (WRT) modular transformation behavior and the volume property related to hyperbolic knot theory. Furthermore, our analysis proves the existence of a topological quantum field theory (TQFT) capable of generating $J_n^T$. As a significant outcome of this work, we derive a closed-form expression for the Alexander module associated with $J_n^T$.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) addresses the challenge of selecting the appropriate meaning for polysemous words within a given sentence context. Due to variations in corpus size and whether training and evaluation occur separately (split) or on the full dataset (non-split), performance metrics in WSD benchmarking can fluctuate significantly, often leading to confusion. The objective of the paper is to ensure consistency in benchmarking the Public WSD Task (SenseMaker-WSM 2019) by systematically evaluating standard input features and multiple error reporting strategies. Results indicate that performance is highly sensitive to whether a benchmark is run in split or non-split modes. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that both the test dataset and a specific combination of test features and evaluation methods are necessary for generating reliable, comparable statistics.

This study develops an integral representation for the inverted $\Gamma$ function as a regularized hypersingular real integral. It verifies equivalence with established complex formulations and formulates a associated complex integral representation traversing the canonical Hankel contour.

This study focuses on the challenging cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic parsing task, which relies heavily on both the anticipated and actual SQL features within database schemas. To address this difficulty, we suggest a novel framework that decouples joint semantic decoding and schema mapping into distinct stages. Initially, we decode SEMANTIC trees—representing an intermediate representation of SQL semantics—using an attention-based sequence-to-tree model trained with a specialized derivation score. Subsequently, we map these SEMANTIC trees to specific SQL operators based on these frameworks, enhancing performance across multiple evaluated benchmarks for these questions. We evaluate two distinct variations of this proposed method. The **first** leverages syntax-knowledge-based learning using a semantic tree as an interface to connect these stages, while the **second** employs self-supervised learning using an end-to-end approach to streamline the process. The results demonstrate that the proposed methodology outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines on these benchmarks for these questions.

This paper investigates the deployment of differential privacy within graph-structured environments. It identifies key privacy vulnerabilities in graph processing and establishes the privacy bounds for several standard graph algorithms. Furthermore, the study introduces a novel, straightforward mechanism for adding privacy to directed multigraphs by defining graph structure sensitively. Subsequently, we address graph data that are both differentially private and utility-optimized by introducing a utility-sensitive differential privacy framework. Finally, several graph algorithms are implemented under these private settings to validate the proposed methods through experiments.

The vast array of data from the final phase of the Euclid mission will enable a detailed study of the Milky Way's satellite system, complementing insights gained from nearby system analyses such as those by the Hubble Space Telescope and upcoming surveys like LSST. Due to Euclid's narrow 1 arcminute-wide single-channel imaging mode, its coverage of the Local Group will rely heavily on telescope follow-up observations. However, Euclid's high-resolution 1 arcsecond by 1 arcsecond maps of the Local Group, combined with its specific spectral capabilities and historical archives, will significantly enhance the calibration of subsequent surveys. These synergies, along with Euclid's gravitational lensing measurements on the halo, will collectively constrain the satellite dark matter substructure. Furthermore, the mission is well-suited for detecting point sources within the satellite system, including core-collapsed globular clusters, stellar remnants, and active galactic nuclei, as Euclid's 1-Jansky sensitivity targets an flux range of 0.17-Jansky to 3.0-Jansky (in the Vega system).

This study presents a novel framework for the automated generation of roads in virtual testing environments, utilizing parameterized functional mappings to create network-wide parametric geometry driven by control points. By leveraging these parameters, we establish a method to virtually adjust the geometric features of test field road networks through alterations to specific control points. We propose a new semantic mapping between parametric geometric functions and functional attributes, enabling engineers to craft challenging and diverse testing scenarios with greater ease. Furthermore, we introduce standardized protocols for describing parametric geometry and conclude with the development of an open-source reference implementation.

Descriptions are frequently offered alongside suggestions to support user discovery, yet recommending auto-generated playlists (like personalized ones) raises the challenge of creating appropriate descriptions for entire collections. This paper presents a method for constructing these descriptions through "music captioning." Our proposed approach employs both feature-level and semantic representations to learn the mapping from a playlist description text to the constituent tracks. Conversely, descriptions can be described by reversing this process: given a text description, the system recommends tracks that match. We assess our method using the Spotify dataset and achieve superior results compared to existing baselines.

Hydrodynamic theories have recently gained traction for simulating the dynamics of quantum many-body systems, particularly interacting Bose gases, yet these approaches encounter difficulties when applied to highly quantum regimes or scenarios involving low particle densities. To overcome these limitations, we present a novel stochastic hydrodynamic framework grounded in the positive-P phase-space representation, a method exact for coherent-state quantum Bose gases. This proposed stochastichydrodynamic method enables the efficient simulation of the exact dynamics within the quantum Bose model. Furthermore, this research introduces a universal stochastic scaling hypothesis applicable to quantum phase transitions driven by tunable interaction strengths. Leveraging this hypothesis, our methodology proves exceptionally effective in accelerating the convergence of numerical simulations across dynamical quantum phase transitions occurring within the Bose-Hubbard model.

Long-lasting, highly intermittent localized structures known as "blobs" appear in the edge plasma of the Tokamaks. These phenomena are characterized by significant transport of floating potential and ion saturation current, along with the carrying of parallel currents. This study introduces a novel technique utilizing a double probe circuit to measure the time-averaged ion saturation current in the blob core, which is subsequently compared against standard single probe voltages and Langmuir diagnostic data. The results indicate that localized circuits with double probes detect current peaks roughly an order of magnitude greater than those recorded by single probe systems when encountering the same structures. This discrepancy is attributed to the reduced input impedance of the double probe configuration, which allows for more effective detection of the currents inherent in these events. Consequently, these findings suggest that current-bearing blobs may occur with a frequency several times higher than what traditional single probe diagnostics reveal. Consequently, existing methodologies for analyzing blob statistics likely underestimate both the magnitude and frequency of localized events in the boundary layer.

If the discrete-time annealed large deviation principle (LDP) holds for a pair of dynamical systems $(\sigma, T)$ on a standard Borel space $M$ under an LDP-satisfying correspondence $f: M \to \mathbb{R}$, then the continuous-time system $(\sigma_t, T_t)$ obeys an annealed LDP with a rate function $\!I_T^{\text{ann}}$ related to the infimum of specific relative entropies within level sets of $f$. Furthermore, should a pair of systems $(\sigma, T)$ support a unique eigenvalue gap dynamics (E.D.G.) and satisfy the annealed large deviation principle for $f$, the continuous-time process $(\sigma_t, T_t)$ generates a contractive semi-group of operators $(P_t)_{t \ge 0}$; this process displays a large deviation principle (LD P) with a good rate function $I$. Notably, if $(\sigma, T)$ is a Bernoulli system, this principle extends (under suitable conditions) to the setting of relative entropy.

Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology has recently gained prominence in wireless communications and radar systems due to the advantages offered by wirewalls, mesh antennas, and similar environments toward target parameter estimation. Nevertheless, most existing studies on radar-IRS configurations rely on line-of-sight (LoS) paths between the surface and both the target and the radar transmitter/receiver. In practice, however, IRS surfaces often encounter numerous obstacles that block direct links with targets or radar equipment, making non-line-of-sight (NLoS) interaction essential for effective integration. Consequently, this paper introduces a novel intelligent reflecting surface-assisted radar system operating under non-line-of-sight conditions. This model facilitates bidirectional communication, enabling the surface to interact reflectively with targets even when direct links are unavailable. Specifically, the model presents a dual-IRS architecture in which two surfaces reflect incident signals from both the target and the radar equipment in reverse, allowing for parameter estimation based on cross-correlation. Furthermore, the study derives closed-form expressions for key metrics including the probability of escape, mean squared error, and Cramér-Rao lower bounds. Validation through numerical results demonstrates the effectiveness and utility of the proposed non-line-of-sight radar-IRS system.

Fuzzing stands as a potent technique for uncovering software bugs, yet its efficacy in exposing memory safety vulnerabilities is frequently hampered by issues like program termination through exceptions or assertion failures. This paper introduces a comprehensive mutation analysis framework designed to automatically generate fuzzing inputs specifically crafted to bypass such non-terminating terminating errors, thereby facilitating fuzz-driven fault detection. Our approach leverages symbolic execution to generate test cases capable of navigating around these safety checks. To optimize resource usage, we employ a learning-based strategy to narrow the scope of this analysis. Furthermore, to maximize the efficiency of input generation, we developed a corresponding fuzzing engine tailored for our purposes. The practical implementation of this method, known as MutAri, has been made accessible via an open-source fuzzing environment called AFL-mut. Evaluations conducted on real-world targets using MutAri demonstrate its practicality and robustness.

This study introduces CoReL, an efficient approach for continual learning in image classification that utilizes frozen, pre-trained models. In the context of continual learning, the challenge of acquiring new data while accessing prior datasets is often impractical; consequently, this work focuses on the limitation of unavailable old data for training. We evaluate the model using the CIFAR-100 dataset, treating it as a setting where historical data cannot be reused. Our findings indicate that CoRe enhances performance in such scenarios when compared to other frozen model strategies. Furthermore, the study explores a comparison between full fine-tuning and the use of a feature extractor, offering insights into the trade-offs between computational efficiency and accuracy. The proposed method employs a lightweight, pre-trained classifier trained on existing features to mitigate the impact of limited data volume. We extract features via a frozen, large-scale model and then fine-tune these features with a small number of newly acquired features from the target task. Specifically, we use a small number of low-dimensional feature representations (e.g., global pooling) to generate task-specific outputs via a lightweight classifier head. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Continual CIFAR-100/1000/10000/100000/1000000/10000000000000000000000000000000000

This work addresses the long-standing problem of determining local Hölder regularity for area-minimizing surfaces within the fractional setting. We introduce the concept of a fractional minimal surface by establishing a fractional version of the Bernstein theorem and deriving estimates for second derivatives for surfaces with small, fixed support. Additionally, we investigate regularity issues associated with minimal surfaces defined by variational inequalities involving fractional operators.

This section serves as our findings' summary. In this work, we examine a semilinear parabolic system:

$$
\begin{cases}
u_t = \Delta u + f(u), & \text{in } \Omega \times (0,T), \\
u = 0, & \text{on } \partial\Omega \times (0,T),
\end{cases}
$$

where $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n \geq 2$) represents a bounded domain with a smooth boundary, and $f \in C^2(\mathbb{R})$. Our primary focus lies in solutions exhibiting quasiconvergence but lacking convergence. Assuming the existence of a non-degenerate critical point $c \in \mathbb{R}$, we demonstrate that any global solution $u$ which fails to converge as $t \to \infty$ must converge as $t \to \infty$ to a steady state, provided either $f$ satisfies the local Lipschitz condition near $c$, or specific conditions regarding the linearized system's spectrum at $c$ are satisfied. Our methodology integrates techniques from ordinary differential equations, such as constructing Lyapunov functionals, alongside those from the theory of the local Lipschitz condition.

The configuration of low-lying spin states in $^{64}$Ni is examined, with particular attention to findings from the NIST $\gamma$-ray Nuclear Array. This extensive dataset, compiled over several decades, is compared against previous measurements to ensure a more rigorous analysis. The results indicate the identification of four new excited states within the J$\pi$ = 0+ ground state band, with energies falling between 1.5 and 2.5 MeV. Additionally, the study adds seven previously unknown levels to the known database, bringing the count of unassigned states in this region down to just one.

This study investigates the computational difficulty of locating equilibria in $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, where the payoff functions vary with a Lipschitz constant $\frac{n\alpha}{\theta}$ relative to a single player's deviation. We introduce a randomized algorithm that locates an $\epsilon$-approximate $m$-cyclic weak equilibrium in a $d$-dimensional domain volume $d$ in time $O_{\epsilon,d}$ ($t_{\alpha}$) per dimension, requiring time proportional to $n\alpha$ per dimension. Conversely, under randomized complexity assumptions, we demonstrate that approximating the finding of weak equilibria in any $\epsilon$ factor for any dimensionless games is computationally difficult. This result is tight as it matches known lower bounds.

K-fold cross-validation is a prevalent technique for cross-validation and parameter optimization in machine learning. However, the high cost incurred by multiple model trainings and evaluations during this process frequently results in suboptimal parameter selection. To address this, this paper introduces a novel approach called K-Fold Shrinkage that reduces error estimates through the aggregation of K-fold results via shrinkage. By utilizing the resulting insights, we demonstrate that K-Fold Shrinkage successfully identifies superior hyperparameters compared to traditional methods, particularly in the context of Random Forest construction. Experimental results confirm that this approach not only achieves these gains but also significantly lowers computational expenses relative to standard K-fold cross-validation.

Deep Neural Networks have demonstrated remarkable success across a wide spectrum of tasks in knowledge learning, with applications ranging from computer vision and natural language processing to speech recognition and knowledge inference. Although these models are typically data-hungry, recent innovations in distillation architectures known as Teacher-Student frameworks enable the acquisition of knowledge from implicit deep sources without explicit retraining. These student networks can be more efficient and compact, inheriting the expertise of larger teacher networks through mechanisms like ensemble methods and attention mechanisms, which enhance both student performance and computational efficiency. While such distillation techniques yield tangible results, they often suffer from a lack of interpretability and transparency, hindering trust and adoption in mission-critical environments. To address this gap, our work introduces a novel framework called Graph-based Graphical Models (GGM) for Graph-Based Attention (GBA) that enables the extraction of sparse, structured, and explicit rules from the internal weights of a Graph Neural Network (GCN). By applying our method to two distinct datasets, we demonstrate that our approach not only improves the accuracy of the student model but also significantly enhances its model performance.

This paper introduces a novel framework for graphical model inference where states and transitions are parameterized by functions drawn from predefined libraries. We employ deterministic finite state automata (DFSAs) selected from this library to symbolically represent the system's transition dynamics. Each state within a DFSFA associates with a distinct symbol set, which defines the state transition vectors. By utilizing DFSAs, we group together symbol sequences that correspond to identical transitions, allowing us to reuse previously computed operations and cache results. We detail the construction method for such systems and present an efficient algorithm designed to find optimal trajectories by moving through data partitions. Experimental evaluations confirm that this approach accelerates the inference process without any sacrifice in trajectory optimality.

We calculate the photon recoil effects on the absorption profile of light within an ultracold gas, utilizing linear response theory and Monte Carlo integration to handle photon statistics. The photon recoil induces a parabolic asymmetry within the absorption profile, with the associated red shift increasing with photon intensity. These findings may have significant implications for interpreting photodetection measurements and optimizing laser frequency stabilization via optical pumping cavities.

Dramatic, rapid shifts in the flow and mechanical behavior of dense suspensions occur when exposed to sufficiently high shear stress, moving from viscous to glassy behavior. Although experimental data and simulations have individually mapped this shear- viscous to glass transition trajectory, a comprehensive explanation has been absent. We demonstrate that this transition is driven by a crossover in the characteristic length and time scales of particle interactions: from multi-body hydrodynamic interactions to short-range contact-based mechanisms. This process is quantified by a single continuous parameter encompassing stress and stress. Using a combination of scattering methods, tomography, and computational modeling, we reveal that the elastic mechanical response of the suspension remains continuous across the transition and is primarily dictated by the material's viscosity. Conversely, micro-structural analysis indicates the suspension's compressive modulus is non-monotonic, initially climbing before declining as shear stress intensifies. These insights provide a foundational understanding for tailoring the properties of dense suspensions.

We present findings indicating that low-lying triplon excitations within bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnets offer a viable pathway for realizing twisted superfluid and supersolid phases. By constructing a twoplant Helensian antiferomagnetic model, I demonstrate through field theoretical approaches that sufficient spatially dependent Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions can induce these phases in both individual layers individually and across the system as a whole, with the transition threshold determined specifically by the magnitude of these interactions relative to the intralayer coupling strength. Further analysis of two- and three-tion excitation entropy reveals the emergence of long-range order in the fluid and superfluid states, respectively, while calculations of specific heat and the correlation functions support these theoretical outcomes by reflecting the characteristic features of the twisted superfluid and twisted supersolid phases.

This work examines the scattering probability of WIMPs in direct detection experiments, quantifying it via the average number of WIMP-Wiggle interactions per nuclear recoil event. We demonstrate that this probability is not uniform across the recoil spectrum but varies significantly with nuclear recoil energy and scattering angle. By incorporating various nuclear recoil energy distributions and angle-dependent models, we illustrate how these non-uniformities shape the observed scattering probability spectrum. Additionally, we analyze the sensitivity of different direct detection experiments to these non-uniform effects.

This study proposes the advancement of an intense, polarized, circular electron-positron source, enabling new high-luminosity collision setups with protons and nuclei (an electron-proton/nucleus collider). Such a facility, utilizing the proposed $e^{\mp} \mu^{\pm}$ beam pair, would serve as a versatile tool for addressing fundamental questions in both nuclear and particle physics. The report specifically examines the generation of rare, high-transverse-momentum positrons capable of initiating hard scattering events when paired with large nuclear targets. Furthermore, in an environment of high positron flux, the device functions as a precision instrument for determining the running value of the strong coupling constant, $\alpha_s(q^2)$, across diverse momentum scales ($q^2$).

Although respiratory motion compensation is vital for MRI scans, existing methods often rely on breath-holding or are limited to small Field-of-View (FOV) applications. We propose a novel framework utilizing a longley shortley (LSI) technique, which involves acquiring multiple shifted FOVs sequentially to reconstruct a complete image. By aligning these shifted FOVs, the system achieves motion compensation. However, sequential acquisition in traditional sequences results in motion artifacts in k-space due to long repetition times (TR), degrading image quality. To resolve this, we introduce a novel multi-echo gradient-recalled echo (MEGRE) sequence that captures several FOVs per TR. This approach captures multiple phase-contrast MEGRE datasets per FOV, each with a distinct echo time (TE) tailored to create a fully or partially T2*-weighted image. By assigning specific FOVs to specific TEs, the framework ensures optimal utilization of data across motion states and contrast requirements. Evaluation via phantom studies and in vivo experiments confirms the approach's efficacy, demonstrating superior performance compared to conventional free-breathing T2*-weighted imaging.

This paper proposes an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function (ICCBF) technique to synthesize safe controls for non-linear control systems subject to constraints. An ICCBF guarantees forward invariance of a safe set by ensuring that, from any state near the boundary, a safety-preserving control input exists within a finite time. We introduce a broad class of feedback controls that achieve this, adapting existing approaches by incorporating constraints to prevent violation. Convergence properties are established, and the framework is extended to systems with output feedback by integrating it with localized observers. Simulation results validate the proposed method.

This study introduces the novel concept of CF-approximation spaces via the framework of CF-approximable structures. We define CF-topologies on these spaces and establish an isomorphism between the category of CF-approximation spaces and the category of CF-topological spaces, utilizing the derived CF-topological structure and induced CF-topologies respectively. Furthermore, through the lens of CF-approximable structures, it is demonstrated that the category of CF-approximation spaces is equivalent to the category of CF-latticed proximity spaces, with the associated CF-latticed proximity derived specifically as its CF-latticed proximity structure. Finally, by means of CF-approximable CF-relations, a one-way mapping is established indicating that CF-relations are sufficient to generate a CF-approximable CF-topological structure.

Statistical significance testing is essential for evaluating and comparing natural language processing systems. Among various methods, the paired-permutation test stands out for its robustness, simplicity, and ability to control error rates. However, these advantages have often limited its adoption due to difficult implementations and calculations. This article presents an easily accessible R-based package that computes this test—featuring statistical significance estimates via a bootstrap approach and significant results determination through p-values—for various metric types. Additionally, it offers standardized tools to evaluate common NLP tasks, such as machine translation and text classification. All assets required to utilize this package, including the computing code and bootstrap algorithms, are available as open-source on GitHub.

Graph neural networks have demonstrated significant efficacy in addressing diverse tasks across various domains. A critical challenge in deploying these models is their sensitivity to graph structural perturbations, which complicates knowledge transfer and model ensembling. Addressing this, we introduce a graph structural refinement approach that enhances model accuracy through distillation and aggregation. We propose a combined strategy leveraging contrastive learning and parameterized modules to improve result consistency. Specifically, our method employs an auxiliary module to generate structural updates via knowledge distillation, while a contrastive module ensures the stability of these modifications. Experiments on four datasets confirm that this approach reduces structural edge counts by approximately 30% while maintaining comparable model accuracy.

CountSketch serves as a method for creating sketches of high-dimensional data vectors, enabling the approximation of their inner products with other data vectors while supporting various other computational tasks. This study introduces an enhanced version of CountSketch, termed CountDeepSketch, which leverages multiple CountSketch instances to further refine the quality of these projections. This new approach offers improved performance for inner product estimation and facilitates more accurate solutions to underdetermined linear systems. Additionally, CountDeepSketch is adapted specifically for estimating heavy hitters with higher accuracy. We evaluate its performance through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

In a liquid of superconducting vortices, a transverse electric field is produced by a longitudinal temperature gradient, representing the Nernst effect, which reaches a maximum at moderate temperatures and fields. This peak height and its broad profile suggest an underlying dominant timescale governing the motion of vortex bundles. This finding is interpreted through a model of vortex dynamics that accounts for multiple mechanisms of dissipation.

Aggregators play a critical role in the effective integration of distributed generators and load fluctuations into power systems. To do so, distributed generators must be controllable, while aggregating load variations requires actionable thresholds. This paper examines the limits of detectable (aggregatable) load changes from the user perspective, defining clear criteria for when a generation shift can actually be observed monitoring systems. Based on these principles, we develop a new generation aggregation technique using penalized predictive control (PPC), which leveraged frequency data and combines multiple generation sources. The method incorporates optimization strategies tailored to small, incremental adjustments as well as steps to improve solutions over time, alongside adjustments for real-world constraints and biases. Simulations using historical U.S. electricity consumption data demonstrate that this approach effectively manages generation on a massive scale, handling more than a 1000 times the number of generators managed by current technology, resulting in significantly higher frequency stability.

This paper examines the impact of online news on stock market dynamics. Specifically, it investigates whether the quantity, topic, sentiment, and headline text of web news influence stock prices.
