Existing methods typically rely on the templates' visual structures to guide the extraction process, employing either rule-based algorithms or neural networks. While these methods are effective on clean, digital versions of templates, their performance degrades substantially when applied to physical image scans. This paper introduces Template2Text, a method designed to convert low-quality image scans of templates into textual data. Our proposed approach leverages a diffusion-based generative model to generate high-fidelity image templates directly from their corresponding rough, low-resolution images, thereby substantially improving extraction performance. Furthermore, we present a new dataset comprising over 1,000 real-world form image templates across diverse generative structures. Empirical results demonstrate that combining Template2Text with a previously established visual-to-text extraction method reduces the F1 score gap between degraded and digital versions of master templates by 13.8%. Finally, we release a user-friendly web interface for interacting with the system.

Accurately quantifying polarization is essential for analyzing how societies function. This paper evaluates three prominent polarization measurement approaches—Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt), Two Partite (TWP), and Partite with Entropy (TWP-ENT)—within a binary context using simulations. The TWP-ENT method combines TWP principles with entropy-based measurement. A key innovation involves applying a normalization technique to these measures to mitigate the impact of distributional differences. Simulation results indicate that except for TWP-ENT, standard normalization significantly degrades the accuracy of MaxEnt and TWP compared to unnormalized versions, whereas accuracy for TWP-ENT remains largely unaffected. In contrast, when applied to a real-world social network, the normalized measures yield more accurate outcomes than unnormalized ones due to the presence of polarization beyond the binary context; however, this study restricts its focus strictly to binary measurements. Given these findings, the paper recommends against using normalized measures for binary tasks while suggesting their adoption for non-barycentric (multidimensional) cases.

Multilayer networks offer a more realistic depiction of complex system dynamics compared to single-layer alternatives, yet their analysis remains challenging due to an abundance of possible inter-layer connectivity configurations. This study presents an analytical investigation into the synchronization of multilayer networks, examining various coupling architectures across multiple layers. Although numerous inter-layer topologies were modeled, our results indicate that synchronization performance depends primarily on the aggregate node degree distribution and the intrinsic synchronization dynamics of each layer, with minimal sensitivity to specific inter-layer connection details. To achieve this, we developed a novel theoretical framework capable of handling general network motifs and coupling schemes while operating under broad assumptions. On average, our approach demonstrates that multilayer networks synchronize significantly faster than single-layer networks containing an equivalent total number of nodes. This finding holds true regardless of whether coupling is implemented between a single anchor layer and others or via a complex mesh of interconnections. Ultimately, our approach provides a straightforward and efficient tool for evaluating synchronization in systems where network structures and coupling schemes are diverse.

Formal verification techniques are increasingly integrated into software quality assurance workflows, evolving from exclusive tools for life-critical systems to essential components within continuous feedback loops on a regular schedule. This shift requires a thorough examination of emerging research trends, the practical challenges encountered in regular testing environments, and the methodologies needed to manage formal verification efforts effectively under such conditions. The manuscript begins by outlining the scope of formal testing and integration within continuous testing frameworks, subsequently reviews relevant literature, and concludes by proposing research avenues to further advance the field.

Prompt Tuning has recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for parameter-efficient adaptation of large pre-trained models. In this paper, we investigate HyperPrompt, an innovative approach utilizing hyper-prompts to create task-specific feature representations within the input embeddings space of language models. HyperPrompt integrates three distinct types of learnable hyper-prompts designed for varied task objectives: (1) HyperHyPa, which are hyper-prompts that generate other types of hyper-prompts; (2) HyperHyLoc, which generate position encodings to inject positional information into the model; and (3) HyperHyAtt, which generate attention patterns to modify self-attention mechanisms. Crucially, HyperPrompts operate by generating task-tailored prompt structures that adapt both positional and attentional dynamics, facilitating highly effective feature mapping. Extensive experiments across ten natural language inference tasks demonstrate that HyperPrompts significantly enhance performance by up to 5.3 percentage points compared to other prompt tuning strategies and recover 94.9% of the performance of frozen large language models. Additionally, HyperPrompts exhibit distinct advantages in reducing catastrophic forgetting. Overall, these contributions establish HyperPrompts as a versatile and high-performance framework for adapting large language models to specific downstream tasks.

The associated boundary states display distinct, universal critical exponents. Furthermore, the model is analytically connected to the chiral critical theory describing its boundary. The universal critical exponent derived from this theory aligns precisely with the central charge characterizing the dynamical critical transitions separating bulk and boundary states. This work addresses the task of finding a majority element in a fully connected network where a fraction of participants act maliciously. A flat, decentralized algorithm is proposed to withstand up to $\frac{n}{4} - 1$ Byzantine actors among $n$ total nodes, a level of resilience previously unattainable by any decentralized approach. Although the method operates within $O(\log^2 n)$ time steps on theoretical models matching Bitcoin's characteristics, its practical execution proves orders of magnitude faster. By integrating this algorithm with a consensus protocol capable of confirming majority status, the construction of a voting system emerges, offering a low-memory, lightweight, and decentralized alternative to existing technologies like Bitcoin for digital voting applications.

Accurate traffic control depends on effectively estimating traffic states. This research proposes a nonparametric method for estimating queue lengths at traffic signals by leveraging probe vehicle loop flow-time (FT) trajectories. First, the study establishes that, between two consecutive signal phases, FT data follows a Pareto distribution. Conditional queue length distributions are then estimated using the parameters of the FT model via Bayesian inference. Performance evaluation through both real-world implementation and simulation demonstrates that this approach is feasible and outperforms existing methods, particularly in scenarios with sparse probe vehicle coverage.

Quantum annealing serves as a method for resolving combinatorial optimization problems by integrating them into the ground state of a quantum system. Although significant commercial interest in this approach has grown, questions remain regarding its efficacy, particularly concerning the inclusion of anti-ferromagnetic interactions. These elements are excluded from current annealing-based commercial hardware due to the inability to generate such interactions physically in the required transverse fields. This study demonstrates that anti-ferromagnetic interactions enable quantum annealing to overcome obstacles inherent in problem Hamiltonians, specifically bottlenecks caused by large energy gaps. We introduce a class of problem instances where these interactions allow finding exact ground states via efficient quantum paths, contrasting sharply with the exponential time duration necessitated by standard annealing methods in their absence. Additionally, we establish a polynomial-time solution for problem instances featuring three-spin rings, a result that may extend to more generalized systems. Ultimately, our contribution offers insight into the broader utility of quantum annealing for specific subsets of optimization challenges.

We propose Locally Critic Attested Training (LoCAT), a novel method designed to counter data poisoning in federated learning. In this framework, the global model acts as a local critic for each participating data source. During each round of communication, clients submit multiple potential updates corresponding to distinct layers of the global model. LoCAT employs statistical hypothesis testing to verify, after every round, whether each provided update represents genuine learning from the respective local data. We establish a strong connection between this hypothesis testing approach and the risk of falsely accepting poisoned model components, thereby ensuring effective detection. To further streamline the process, we introduce an accelerated variant of LoCAT that significantly reduces the time required per communication iteration while maintaining robust anti-poisoning capabilities. Extensive experiments across several standard benchmarks confirm that LoOUT successfully identifies poisoned updates with high precision and recall, even when malicious agents contribute up to 90% of the total data.

Fiber-reinforced composite materials are renowned for their exceptional mechanical attributes, such as high specific strength and stiffness, yet these same traits render them opaque to traditional visual inspection for damage assessment. This paper introduces a method for assessing damage in such materials by integrating a conductive polymer matrix with carbon nanotubes to create an electrically conductive network susceptible to disruption by structural failures. The sensing principle relies on monitoring variations in the material's electrical conductivity; specifically, the rate of change in conductivity correlates with the loss of mass following impact events. This sensitivity to conductivity changes enables the identification of both visible surface damages and subsinternal delamination. An additional benefit of this approach is its capability to function as a low-cost, self-powered indicator of damage location.

We challenge ourselves with a new problem rooted in statistical mechanics and cooperative game theory: investigating how individual wisdom translates into collective insight within an social agent population. Our setting involves an unbounded board game where a team collaborates to secure the highest possible score. We examine an evolutionary framework where agents compete for replication, utilizing a fitness measure grounded in a game's rank-order correlations. Our findings reveal a phase transition marking the shift from solitary to collaborative play. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a cooperative evolutionary system not only outperforms an evolutionary solitary one but also achieves a higher scores than any solitary environment.

We present a learning-based control algorithm designed for unknown dynamical systems operating under extreme data constraints. Specifically, the method relies on accessing only a single noisy trajectory from an arbitrary starting point within an environment defined by a compact state space, utilizing no prior process models and incorporating minimal side information. Leveraging such auxiliary cues to accelerate system exploration is recognized as particularly valuable, a notion we formalize as the learning cost—the quantity of noise required to drive a system to a target state with guaranteed certainty. We demonstrate that our approach ensures control is learned within this logarithmic noise threshold guarantee, a result that holds true regardless of the system's dynamics. Furthermore, numerical simulations confirm the method's robustness when applied to systems with continuous state spaces.

We examine a scenario within a three-neutrino framework that includes interactions with a fourth sterile neutrino, where the sterile neutrino is a mixture of CP-even and CP-odd states. In this model, CP-protected sterile oscillations can generate visible signs of LSND and MiniBoone anomalies, while simultaneously ensuring long durations and distances for sterile neutrinos from creation to decay due to effects like visible decay power suppression. However, if the neutrino-type Majorana CP eigenstate is selected, these long lifetimes are restricted to specific energy ranges. Furthermore, if the lightest neutrino is established as a CP-mixed state, this model offers observable signatures at future colliders and lepton collision facilities.

This study examines the submission patterns of university-level physics homework from Fall 2019 to Spring 2021, a period disrupted by remote learning necessitated by the COVID-19 pandemic. The participant pool consisted of 11,820 students, with the submissions data of 5,914 first-generation college entrants serving as the primary focus. The analysis highlights distinct differences between first and non-first generations regarding homework attempt frequency, frequency of multiple submissions per problem, and the timing of their submissions. These behavioral disparities were largely unaffected by the pandemic-induced shift to online instruction. The authors argue that such patterns reflect deep-seated differences in academic self-confidence and resource accessibility, rather than the temporary challenges of remote learning. Consequently, grading algorithms designed to evaluate homework submissions must account for these variations to ensure fairness toward first-generation students.

Unlike Liouville theory, where such computations rely heavily on special functions and exact solvability, extending these calculations to higher values of the Toda charge $n$ is not feasible. Instead, we utilize the framework of semiclassical large-$c$ expansions, which is valid when the central charge $c$ is large relative to central terms. Within this regime, we employ WKB approximations to derive computationally manageable results. Our analysis reveals that the required mathematical apparatus extends significantly beyond standard Lie algebraic structures, necessitating insights from higher algebraic theories, specifically the $A_n$-type theory of gerstenhaber.

The dynamics of the non-extremal Reissner-Nordstr$\ddot{o}$m black hole in the AdS spacetime are investigated within the framework of semiclassical gravity. By determining the semi-classical metric through perturbation theory, where corrections to the standard Einstein equations are incorporated, we calculate both thermodynamic and mechanical quantities for the non-extremial case. The analysis demonstrates that the non-extremial interpretation relies on the magnitude of the horizon radius relative to the non-extremality parameter: specifically, if the mechanical horizon radius is smaller than the thermodynamic one, the non-extremality cannot be dismissed, whereas the converse implies it can be avoided. Furthermore, we show that incorporating these quantum corrections either eliminates or induces naked singularities within specific parameter regimes.

This work introduces a new formalization of set theory grounded in both paracomplete and paraconsistent logic, operating within a four-valued framework where statements can be true, false, both true and false, or neither true nor false. It introduces the Axiom of Choice as a default assumption that is not necessarily true or false, while defining standard ZFC axioms as requiring only truth. The framework defines a novel, intuitionistic-style semantic model based on a three-sorted structure. Within this system, the concepts of consistency and decidability are re-established, and it is demonstrated that the classic Lindelöf theorem and Tarski-Cantor mostowskic cardinality conclusions remain valid. Finally, the authors establish a revised, intuitive version of Gödel's incompleteness theorems suitable for this setting.

Phylogenetic networks capture the evolutionary trajectories of species while accounting for intricate events like horizontal gene transfer and gene recombination, offering a more detailed view of history than standard phylogenetic trees, which depict only divergence. Despite their utility, visualizing and analyzing these structures poses significant challenges due to their complex, web-like visual representation. This paper introduces a new data structure called the Phylogenetic Network List (PNL) designed to store networks in main memory and facilitate efficient querying. We also developed algorithms to extract subgraphs from PNLs, enabling effective visualization and analysis of evolutionary subsets. Performance evaluations confirm that our approach drastically reduces response times for common operations on real-world datasets compared to database systems and standard file formats.

Animals move for various reasons, including searching for food, avoiding harm, and reproducing. While the aim of this work is to introduce a new general-purpose framework for modeling animal motion, a primary focus remains on locomotor behavior found in marine species. Although these exist across all taxonomic divisions, researchers have extensively studied them due to their accessibility and the wealth of available data. Although prior efforts have addressed modeling within this field, they typically target only a limited set of related species. Different from these approaches, this research seeks to establish an open and modular foundation capable of representing animal movement patterns seen in all marine classes. To achieve this, the proposed system integrates insights and existing models from current research while remaining open and modular. Distinctively, it incorporates probabilistic components to account for individual variability and environmental factors, as well as parameters to account for differences among individuals and species-specific variations. Finally, the validity and applicability of this framework are evaluated through an analysis of three diverse marine animal models.

Advancements in hardware-accelerated computing have enabled the acceleration of numerical methods, creating new opportunities for implementing them within signal processing. While classic direct inversion techniques like Gaussian elimination and matrix factorization remain popular, iterative algorithms offer distinct advantages, such as requiring less memory and adapting well to changes. Consequently, there is a need to closely examine these methods, assess their suitability for modern hardware, and understand their behavior when solving large, dense linear systems arising from overdetermined problems. This study provides a close analysis of iterative solution strategies for matrix inversion, with a specific focus on computational complexity, memory usage, and accuracy relative to direct methods. It also explores the application of these techniques to the least squares problem, highlighting the benefits of factorization and iteration in real-time signal processing contexts made possible by today's rapid computing capabilities.

In systems with random scattering, a deposition matrix converts the incoming wavefront into an internal field distribution within the medium. Previously, the corresponding matrix for a one-dimensional system was derived and utilized to analyze how one-dimensional (1D) and two- and three-dimensional (2D and 3D) structures enhance wavefront control and mitigate coherence decay. This paper generalizes that control matrix to arbitrary geometries by integrating it with the Born approximation. Findings indicate that deposition patterns converge rapidly as the number of scattering obstacles increases, allowing for effective parameterization via low-order matrices. Furthermore, experimental results suggest that real-world disordered systems, such as colloidal assemblies, possess sufficient long-range order to simplify the applicable model. Finally, the study establishes a distinct hierarchy among 1D, 2D, and 3D configurations based on their respective randomness levels.

Various physical factors, such as spatially varying potentials or lattice deformations, can trigger topological phase transitions in systems lacking inversion symmetry. One phenomenon arising from these inducements is the topological Anderson insulating phase, named after the symmetry-breaking potential Anderson localizes electrons while the symmetry-preserving symmetric case yields topologically non-trivial states. This work investigates the topological phase transition induced by symmetry breaking in a two-dimensional Dirac material, specifically a graphene monolayer subjected to both symmetry-inducing and inducing fluctuations. We find that such a transition occurs even when the symmetry-inducing fluctuations are weak, provided the symmetry-breaking fluctuations are sufficiently strong. Notably, this induced topological phase is characterized by a negative Chern number, whereas the Anderson topological phase exhibits a negative Chern number, implying the presence of anomalous Hall conductivity in these regimes.

We investigate the genus-one curves that appear in cuts within the elliptic box integral, a genus-one elliptic integral selected for its significance in QCD Feynman integral evaluations due to the rigidity of its associated periods and the patterns in their elliptic diagonals. We determine the free-jacobian invariants by analyzing curve cuts, identifying multiple new families of diagonals previously unreported in the literature. This analysis yields numerous new multi-term diagonals and establishes several general results regarding the genus-one elliptic jacobian, its invariants, and the phenomenon of elliptic dialation.

This work examines a quasi-score-based linearity test for quasi-conditional value-at-risk (qCVaR) in linear models with general, potentially non-convex risk measures. Under the null hypothesis of linearity and assuming parameter identifiability, the corresponding test statistic follows a standard chi-squared distribution asymptotically. Conversely, in alternative hypotheses where parameters are unidentifiable, the asymptotic behavior of the statistic is characterized by a quadratic form involving chi-squared variables, which typically necessitates Monte Carlo methods for asymptotic inference. The efficacy of these tests is confirmed via simulation studies, and their practical implementation is demonstrated using real financial data.

Recent advances in Deep Declarative Networks have enabled differentiating the solution map of parametrized continuous optimization problems, facilitating their integration into end-to-end trainable models. These methods offer efficiency and smoothness benefits compared to discrete, trajectory-based sampling approaches. This paper introduces a broader theoretical framework for deriving gradient formulas for continuous optimization solutions, applicable to scenarios beyond the specific constraint structure found in deep declarative networks. The derived gradient formulas reveal a high dependency on the geometric properties of the optimal manifold. To address this geometric complexity in practical applications, we propose a novel, efficient numerical algorithm for implementing the integrators required by our formulas. Validated through multiple examples and a trajectory prediction task within a reinforcement learning context, the proposed numerical algorithm demonstrates significant speed improvements over existing techniques.

Cellular behaviors, including spreading and migration, are governed by interactions with extracellular signals and regulated via a variety of drugs. Consequently, the integration of live cell video microscopy with the inversion of phase-field models offers a method to screen for compounds that alter specific physical properties. This approach was tested using *Dictyostelium* cells, where drug-induced alterations in cell spreading and motility were analyzed through free energy minimization framework. inverse problem techniques were employed to determine which combinations of energetic parameters best fit experimental live-cell images containing individual cells. The resulting fitted parameters were subsequently compared across different environments and living conditions to illuminate the underlying biological mechanisms. The one-substance tested, amphotericin B, accelerated cell motility despite inhibiting spreading. This observation aligns with the findings from the fitted inverse problem, which indicated substantial reductions in energetic lengthscales. This outcome suggests that phase-field modeling combined with iterative parameter fitting serves as an effective strategy for elucidating how drugs influence the biophysics of cellular processes.

The migration of traditional online malicious activities to blockchain platforms offers cybercriminals the advantages of immutability and decentralization, yet it also introduces new constraints. This study introduces a novel computational model of evolutionarily stable strategies (ESS) specifically designed for blockchain-based fraud. Within this model, criminals face new limitations, including the requirement for on-chain permanence, the need to maintain a consistent historical record, and the necessity of coordinating transactions across multiple accounts to successfully deceive legitimate participants. By incorporating these constraints, our framework allows for the analysis of how both malicious actors and platform users evolve over time. Our findings reveal that while blockchain features can impede certain fraudulent behaviors, they do not inherently guarantee a fraud-free environment. Consequently, this provides a rigorous method for evaluating the potential of blockchain solutions in mitigating cybercrime.

Currently regarded as the sole practical pathway for large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing, the surface code relies on rapid and adaptable decoding algorithms capable of handling experimentally observed faulty syndrome measurements. This paper demonstrates that decoding under fully realistic fault-tolerant constraints can be elegantly recast as a discrete-time, Markovian dynamical system. By leveraging this formulation, we propose a novel decoding approach that drives an learning agent to generate a self-sufficient, adaptive decoding strategy. The effectiveness of this method is validated within the surface code framework, showing its ability to enhance computational efficiency and generalize across varying noise profiles. Furthermore, this methodology is expected to yield significant advantages in other domains involving the decoding of error correction codes with two-dimensional topological structures.

Quantum metrology leverages the principles of quantum mechanics to achieve measurement precision surpassing classical limits, with phase difference determination in interferometry serving as a primary example. Although genuine applications face numerous decoherence challenges, true multi-photon decoherence often remains beneficial for the system. In this work, we analyze the phenomenon where a single photon interacts with a phase shift while an entire Fock state passes through an interferometer. We evaluate performance metrics using classical fidelity, quantum fidelity, and entropy. Furthermore, utilizing a model system composed of two non-interacting atoms and one photon within an interferometer setup, we determine the optimal quantum state for precise phase estimation via both classical and quantum methods. Our analysis reveals that employing an atomic entangled state of [1,1] yields superior classical fidelity and quantum fidelity compared to separable atomic configurations, effectively enabling the achievement of the Heisenberg limit for phase difference measurement accuracy.

Cloud computing offers a promising avenue for HPC workload execution, enabling flexible resource utilization, dynamic scalability, simplified operational management, and optimized costs. However, current cloud providers often deliver subpar performance relative to on-site systems. This study examines the extent to which varying network architectures influence the performance of cloud-based HPC tasks. Our methodology involves running three distinct benchmark suites across four on-site systems and two cloud platforms, encompassing a total of twelve network configurations. Our findings reveal that network architecture is a decisive factor for cloud HPC performance, with specific setups achieving up to 2.5x faster results than others. Furthermore, performance outcomes are highly workload-dependent; for instance, the PaSt benchmark delivered identical results on both analyzed networks, whereas PaCt performance varied significantly. To address this complexity, we introduce a new classification framework organizing benchmarks into four network-sensitive groups based on communication patterns. This classification proves effective in guiding network selection, offering performance improvements of 1.7x to 2.5x depending on the specific benchmark.

Contextual linear bandits represent a well-established framework with significant real-world applications. In this paper, we examine a distributed variation where a coordinator exchanges data with multiple workers, each holding a portion of the context data stream of interest, but receives only statistical summaries of the available data. Our goal involves minimizing regret by selecting suboptimal actions, with decision-making grounded in these exchanged information. Specifically, we address scenarios where bit-level communication constraints apply, allowing the coordinator to request approximately 5 bits per context from each worker. Under these conditions, we introduce learning algorithms grounded in information-theoretic principles. Our contributions include context-dependent lower bounds and corresponding upper limits, which together establish a near-matching framework. This demonstrates that utilizing such minimal information sharing enables workers to enable the coordinator to learn effectively. This is achieved by significantly reducing regret in scenarios where the true parameter vector $\theta^\star$ is sparse, with the remaining components of the context-dependent lower and upper limits being of order $d^{-1}$. This result holds true when the dimensionality $d$ is sufficiently large. In contrast to previous approaches that required access to the true values of $\theta^\star$, our method functions without this true parameter knowledge. This is a significant improvement as the true parameter knowledge is often unavailable or difficult to identify in real-world applications.

The global pandemic necessitated a shift to remote work for everyone, including researchers at Florida State University. Although initially challenging, this arrangement eventually became favorable, allowing us to conduct a survey of our remote work experiences. Utilizing factor analysis, we examined data from 1,000+ valid responses. Our findings indicate that remote work success relies on five core psychological needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness, purpose, and security. Consequently, a needs-fulfillment model was developed to guide future remote work practices. To sustain employee well-being, organizations must ensure these specific needs are met by offering clear objectives, timely feedback, and regular social interactions. Additionally, fostering a sense of meaning and safety requires connecting daily tasks to a broader organizational mission and guaranteeing reliable internet access and functional technology.

We present a calculation of higher-order corrections to higher-order multiperipheral models that explicitly accounts for event-shape dependence. Applying this to $p$+Pb collisions at the LHC, the resulting higher-order contributions to the initial-state effect on the elliptic flow coefficient ($\varepsilon_2$) were evaluated through various event-shape selections. Our analysis indicates that the initial-state effect on the $\Delta \varepsilon_2$ caused by these event shapes is approximately a factor of 2 smaller than recent experimental observations from the ALICE collaboration. This result suggests that higher-order multipoles in the initial spatial anisotropy constitute a crucial, yet often under-estimated, component of the total impact-parameter anisotropy effect on $r\Delta \varepsilon_2$ in single nucleon collisions.

This paper investigates the maximum performance improvement achievable through optimal power control compared to equal power allocation in large interference networks with fixed fixed channels, under both general and binary feedback scenarios. Closed-form solutions are derived for the entremal gain in network models featuring feedback that indicates only whether a sum-rate threshold is exceeded (binary feedback), or no feedback at all. These findings demonstrate that the entremal gain escalates logarithmically with network size and remains essentially unchanged by user count, streamening previous approaches through the use of a lower bound on the superposition of pressure functions. Furthermore, the paper establishes the exact gain environment for any network model that does not provide feedback about specific individual rate outcomes.

This study investigates the influence of stretching the collision timescale ($t_c$) on particle sediment entrainment simulations involving large particles. This approach aims to capture flow and particle dynamics across a broader spectrum of timescales by integrating a smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) model with a low-Mach number Navier-Stokes solver. The research examines two distinct stretching methodologies: one driven by a threshold based on shear stress at the particle interface and another utilizing the instantaneous ratio of the particle relaxation time to the stretching parameter $\alpha$. Results indicate that both methods enhance the realism of particle entrainment and the simulation of turbulence. Specifically, the shear-stress-based approach successfully reproduces experimental sediment entrainment rates, while the $\alpha$-based method yields turbulence kinetic energy levels consistent with laboratory data. Furthermore, the $\alpha$-based stretching produces a flow field characterized by a large recirculation zone upstream of the obstacle and diminished turbulence intensity downstream compared to the unmodified case.

Locomotion using legs on deformable ground presents significant engineering hurdles, primarily stemming from the difficulty of physically modeling soft surfaces and the resulting complex, high-dimensional dynamics that prevent the application of standard control methods. These obstacles make it difficult to create accurate plant models, which in turn hinders effective system design. To address this, the authors propose a model predictive control (MPC) framework designed to stabilize legged vehicles on deformable soil. The approach relies on an abstract grid-based representation of ground deformation, incorporating both continuous and discrete state-space formulations to capture these dynamics. Using this model, the system predicts deformation patterns ahead of the robot's feet to inform control decisions. Validation through simulation demonstrates that this method achieves stable operation across various types of soft terrain.

This manuscript examines the determination of elastic meson form factors within a contact interaction model. Dressed masses for both quarks and mesons are established using gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations. Specifically, the general $M\gamma \to \text{elastic scattering }$ process, where M denotes a two-flavored meson, is analyzed, while charge radii are computed by explicitly evaluating the corresponding form factors for pseudoscalar, axial-vector, vector, and scalar states.

While extensive studies exist regarding the non-contact actuation of oscillating electric fields on the shape spectrum of a suspended water droplet, relatively little attention has been paid to its air-penetrating mode. In this work, such penetration mode serves as a diagnostic tool, through which we demonstrate the potential for selective aerosol removal. Specifically, driving a macroscopic droplet, positioned slightly below its stability point, by electric field variations that shift it across different unstable shape modes allows for targeted particle rejection. This mechanism operates on the principle that aerosols either have insufficient time to reach the droplet surface during rapid oscillations between the concave meniscus state and the conical jet state, or that surface tension forces expel particles that enter during the transition phases. Consequently, this technique enables the filtration of sub-micron to several-micron particles with a size range exceeding three orders of magnitude, achieving an efficiency of approximately 90\% for 1-$\mu$m particles. Furthermore, the system can be adapted to size-select particles; for instance, by stabilizing the droplet in the concave meniscus mode, only small particles adhere while larger particles are rejected.

Negation serves the important function in human language-based communication by expressing negative ideas. In the area of machine translation, deep neural models have demonstrated difficulties accurately learning negation. This paper introduces a novel attention mechanism tailored for handling negation within Sequence-to-Sequence neural translation frameworks. Our approach restructures the encoding process to provide the decoder with explicit information regarding negated elements, rather than relying on the gradual and implicit extraction of negation signals through gradual attention. By implementing this modified attention mechanism, our model shows an improvement in translating sentences containing negation, based on a computational investigation.

Information hierarchies frequently function as structures for navigating and arranging intricate data, yet current methods for automatically generating them from documents remain largely reliant on manual curation. This inadequacy hinders the full advantages offered by advanced natural language processing and computer vision technologies, which could otherwise automatically ingest vast volumes of document content. This paper introduces a framework designed to generate flexible, multi-dimensional information hierarchies in fully automatic fashion. Specifically, it converts the embedding vectors of document titles into a representation that captures their semantic similarity, employing density estimation techniques to delineate distinct cluster assignments. By leveraging these title cluster embeddings, we demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in constructing complex, multi-level hierarchies, significantly enhancing the organizational capabilities compared to existing approaches.

Conformance checking focuses on reconciling recorded behavior derived from event logs against a modeled process definition. Alignments represent a cutting-edge technique for identifying, locating, and quantifying deviations in process executions, specifically traces, relative to reference process models. Currently, alignment methods presuppose complete executions that cover the entire process from start to finish. In reality, however, extracted process executions often fragment into partial paths due to deviations or extraneous activities in case management systems. To address this limitation, this paper introduces Partial Alignment, a novel technique designed to efficiently detect actual process executions within event logs with respect to model-based references. This approach enables the rapid identification of sub-segments within long, process-relevant log paths and their subsequent alignment with model-based alternatives. Additionally, this work details how partial alignments facilitate new metrics for performance evaluation, deviation detection, and the diagnosis of dynamic modeling issues in process engineering contexts.

This study outlines a methodology utilizing the skewness and kurtosis of wave-slope probability distribution tails to calibrate directional significant wave height models. This approach addresses the limitations of relying solely on the linear significant wave height ($H_{s,\rm{lin}}$), which is derived as the slope-weighted mean wave slope. The $H_{s,\rm{lin}}$ is sensitive to the presence of steep waves and exhibits a strong correlation with physical ocean wave parameters, such as whitecapping fluxes and turbulent dissipation rates. By additionally incorporating measures of slope distribution tail skewness and kurtosis, model calibration is significantly improved. The impact of wind sea age on the shape of this tail probability distribution is also examined. The analysis employs a high-quality dataset comprising over 20 million wave slope observations collected via optical sensors at three coastal stations in the North Atlantic.

In software systems, input data is essential for executing functional tests. Regression testing involves re-running tests after modifications to detect any test failures caused by those changes. However, this process often leads to significant resource waste because most existing tests are executed even when only a tiny subset of test data is affected. To address this limitation, we present a methodology for automatically determining which tests must be executed based on recent code changes. Our approach leverages static and dynamic program analysis alongside an understanding of program flow to decide test execution. We evaluated this solution on five real-world applications, demonstrating that it correctly identified changes-irrelevant tests with 96.5% precision and 96.2% recall. Furthermore, our solution reduced total execution time by an average of 76.8%, resulting in substantial financial savings.

In the early phases regarding high-temperature cuprate superconductors, the fundamental mechanisms remained elusive. This study establishes a straightforward empirical connection between a cuprate's interlayer and intralayer magnetic penetration depth ($\lambda_{c}/\lambda_{ab}$) and its electrical resistivity ($\rho_{c}/\rho_{ab}$) near the critical superconducting temperature ($T_c$). By utilizing thin-film techniques to independently assess $\lambda_{c}$ and $ \rho_{c}$, alongside established methods for determining bulk $\lambda_{ab}$ and $\rho_{ab}$, we determined these ratios. Our findings reveal that $\lambda_{c}/\lambda_{ab}$ scales linearly with $ \rho_{c}/\rho_{ab}$ across diverse materials, including those with single- and multi-band characteristics. This relationship holds true whether the linear gap exists on all Fermi surface sheets or only partially, and it remains consistent regardless of whether the linear gap is electron or hole type. Such a direct correlation between a superconductor's magnetic and transport properties offers a significant breakthrough in the field of cuprates.

The paper at hand examines the evolution of dense matter by analyzing the density dependence of the effective sound velocity, $v_e$, within a parametrized framework. This approach aligns observational data regarding the masses and radii of neutron stars with laboratory findings concerning phase transitions at extreme pressures. The study deduces functional forms for $v_e$ and the chemical potential as functions of density ratio, specifically tailoring them to scenarios where $v_e$ either monotonically diminishes or exhibits a minimum. Utilizing these functional formulations, we generate comparative models that closely fit simultaneous observations of the GS21 and PSR J0952-0607, predicting a sharp phase transition occurring at approximately three times the nuclear saturation density ($\approx 3.1\rho_{sat}$). Consequently, a sudden drop in effective sound velocity at very high densities likely signifies such a phase transition, potentially predicting a distinct "maximum mass radius" relation for the neutron star population.

We examine a diverse set of non-classical states, including squeezed and displaced number states, proposing their utility in enhancing sensitivity for specific parameter estimation tasks within a Hadamard interferometer. By analyzing joint purity and von Neumann entropy, we identify equivalent ensembles representing these states. When used together, these states form an ensemble that resists noise more effectively than traditional approaches, resulting in a smaller quantum Fisher information (QFI) bound and thus superior estimation precision for certain parameters. Moreover, the required parameters to define a single-state ensemble member are fewer than those needed for equivalent states in an opposing ensemble, yielding a more compact set of parameters for QFI calculation. Finally, we demonstrate numerically that for specific scenarios, the achieved QFI is maximized, confirming these states' superior performance in parameter estimation.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) functions as a mechanism for angular momentum transport within the inner regions of protoplanetary disks, effectively quenching turbulence. Although the overall impact of dust growth on the VSI is limited in terms of magnitude, this effect becomes increasingly significant in the outer portions of the disks.

The rise of machine learning has brought increased public scrutiny, revealing that malicious actors can embed hidden threats into models. Backdoors are a prevalent form of attack, operating by inserting a secret trigger into the training data that allows an adversary to manipulate predictions while leaving normal operations unaffected. Despite their significance, current defenses remain inadequate, partly because the clandestine nature of the trigger hinders detection. This work introduces a novel framework for locating backdoor triggers that exploits the intrinsic link between an attack's trigger and a deliberately injected high variance within the high-dimensional feature space. In response to this variance, we develop a variance-enhancing transformation that expands these volatile triggers into full-dimensional, heterogeneous variants. Leveraging the resulting diversity, we construct a full-depth variant search pipeline that yields superior quantitative results compared to state-of-the-art methods, successfully identifying even minuscule, encrypted triggers. Our codebase is available at https://github.com/AniruddhaSaxena/BackdoorTriggerHunt.

High-precision astrometry is increasingly vital for Galactic structure research, yet its development faces limitations from unmodeled relativistic effects in astrometric solutions. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of how General Relativity influences Gaia's parallax determination. We demonstrate that paractimetry is particularly sensitive to shifts in the measured barycentric position vector caused by variations in the observed light propagation time. Specifically, if the post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$ deviates from unity, the resulting change in arrival time alters the calculated stellar position by approximately $|\delta\gamma|\approx 10^{-5}$ times the distance to the target. For nearby stars with parallax $\varpi$, this induces a bias in the measured parallax of order $|\delta\gamma|\varpi/2$. To mitigate this, we developed a correction term added to the daily mean reference frame vector in the Gaia data model. Simulation results indicate that incorporating this correction allows for unbiased parallax estimation even with time baselines as short as seven days, provided $|\delta\gamma|$ is kept below $10^{-4}$. Consequently, this improvement is essential for micro-arcsecond level astrometry, especially given Gaia's capability to routinely measure $|\delta\gamma|$ through its quasi-pulsar data analysis.

The proposed method involves optimizing linear and nonlinear layers in tandem, which involves projecting data into a lower-dimensional space and subsequently reconstructing it. Results from a live deployment on a Raspberry Pi model demonstrate significant improvements in both computational time and memory consumption compared to prior state-of-the-art methods.

Using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), we conducted a high-sensitivity neutral hydrogen (HI) survey targeting the nearby spiral galaxy M81. Our data reveals an extended, asymmetric HI disk reaching approximately 95 kpc in radius, with a mean HI column density of $N_{HI} \sim 10^{20} \mbox{ cm}^{-3}$ beyond the galaxy's optical boundary. While the total HI mass calculated from our dataset is $4.1 \pm 0.2 \times 10^{9} M_{\odot}$, the true mass is likely higher given potential gaps in the outermost region. The primary cause of this structural asymmetry is identified as the gravitational interaction with its companion, M81B (M81L), specifically the distortion of M81B's HI disk rather than the one belonging to M81A (M81). The spatial distribution of the outer HI gas closely mirrors the location of a giant HI shell, which coincides with a low-ionization H II region and a spiral density wave, suggesting that shock waves triggered by the interaction drive shell formation and stimulate new star creation. Furthermore, optical and infrared observations indicate no significant star formation within the distant HI structure, implying that while the M81 interaction successfully accretes and extends the galaxy's HI envelope, it currently lacks the conditions to form stars at these outer radii

Utilizing external knowledge to assist machine-based question answering (QA) on tasks requiring commonsense background faces the challenge of overwhelming and noisy data due to the vast volume of irrelevant information. To address this, we introduce a new dataset of 12,885 CommonsenseQA (CQA) alternatives—distractor answers surrounded by relevant semantic context—and train a semantic-comparative model designed to help QA systems identify and select correct responses among these contextualized options. Evaluations reveal that while these more focused, contextualized answer choices significantly boost QA performance, the initial model achieves an additional 5.5% improvement over results obtained using the original uncontextized distractors. Furthermore, analysis indicates that the training regimen induces the model to enhance its capacity for contextual grounding and the extraction of crucial information.

There is a long tradition of research, tracing back to Bachet and Lagrange, concerning whether totally positive elements can always be expressed as a sum of squares. For certain specific structures, such as the integers or polynomials with rational coefficients, decomposition methods are well-established; however, the problem remains largely unresolved for many other significant rings and fields. This study introduces an explicit algorithm that expresses elements in any global field (covering both number fields and global function fields) as a sum of squares with minimal length.

We introduce a compact, rapid, and affordable spectrometer built on a photonics platform, designed to replace the single-grating device commonly used in traditional spectroscopy. Although the resulting spectral data exhibits a lower resolution and reduced signal intensity, the photonics-based system retains the fundamental advantages of being small, fast, and low-cost. We demonstrate the spectrometer's capability in analyzing the emission spectra of plasmas generated by laser-induced breakdown, with our approach offering a novel, cost-effective pathway for applying photonic instruments in diverse fields such as astronomy.

Lately, various machine learning models addressing tasks such as polypharmacy adverse effect recognition, predicting drug interactions, and planning combination treatments have been developed. In this work, we offer a cohesive theoretical perspective on relational machine learning models capable of managing these specific objectives. Furthermore, we analyze prevailing approaches across each category, evaluating their inherent strengths, weaknesses, and applicable use cases. Additionally, key aspects of future research are identified.

This paper introduces a rough path version adapted of an It\^o-Wentzell formula, requiring only a \(\beta\)-H\"older regularity condition where \(\beta \in (\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{2}]\), and simultaneously demands continuous modification of the input signal's integration. It further investigates the continuity of the solution map under these requirements in both the case of fixed and parameter-dependent vector fields. Notably, it addresses the continuity of the map from the driving path to its solution within the topology induced by the Wiener measure.

This work addresses a fundamental challenge in the field of Federated Learning (FL), specifically the difficulty of establishing and verifying assumptions regarding data distribution across network nodes. The proposed framework introduces a comprehensive method to discover and define distributional premises through a democratic inquiry process. This approach is designed to be user-friendly, incurring minimal overhead and remaining entirely decentralised. Implementation details are provided with proofs of concept demonstrating feasibility. This tool is crucial for advancing robust FL nodes, which depend heavily on valid distributional assumptions, ensuring transparency and clarity in these shared prerequisites.

Although rotation-dominated turbulent flows are typically associated with wave dynamics—specifically when the rotation rate far exceeds the characteristic flow frequencies (the regime of wave turbulence)—it is possible to cultivate geostrophic turbulence in rotating systems where wave activity is suppressed ($\text{Ro} \sim O(1)$). This phenomenon was previously demonstrated using a direct numerical simulation (DNS) of the Navier-Stokes equations; however, this study extends the investigation to modelled, physics-informed approaches. We conduct DNS of both wave and vorticity-conserving versions of the Conserved-Quirk Model (CQM) within strong rotation, allowing a direct comparison of the resulting wave-turbulent and wave-turbulence-suppressed regimes. Furthermore, we perform vorticity-conserving CQM simulations across a spectrum of mean rotation rates, simulating the transition from geostrophic turbulence to wave-turbulence-suppressed states. Our simulation results indicate that, within the geostrophic regime, the vorticity-conserving formulation accurately captures both the statistical distributions and dynamical characteristics of turbulence, whereas the standard inqorticity-conserving version underestimates turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) and exhibits incorrect dynamics. Finally, by performing a spectral analysis of the vorticity-conserving CQE, we observe accurate agreement between DNS and simulation regarding TKE anistropy, the Taylor-microscale anistropy, and the presence of a quasi-discrete quantized spectrum featuring a distinct inert

Individuals involved with the criminal justice system frequently exhibit mental health disorders, and courts often mandate treatment as a condition of sentencing. This study analyzes the effects of mandated mental health interventions on recidivism among people on probation within North Carolina courts. Drawing upon variation in court assignments created by randomization within districts, the research utilizes a multistage fixed effects model to isolate causal impacts. The findings indicate that offenders required to undergo mental health therapy during probation are 4 percentage points, or roughly 15 percent fewer likely to reoffend and return to the criminal justice system compared to those not mandated such treatment, even when other factors are accounted for. The reduction in immediate recidvation is substantial, with therapy participants being 9 percent less likely to reoffend within one year; the remaining difference represents a delayed return that takes an average of an additional year compared to the non-therapy group. The paper concludes by discussing the policy implications of these results, particularly the finding that mandated treatment does not merely delay further recurrence.

Pixel-level annotation resources for medical image segmentation are expensive and time-consuming. To alleviate this difficulty, researchers have developed numerous data-efficient methods that leverage pre-trained models and weight sharing to lower demands for annotated data. These strategies, however, often introduce extra complexity and demand significant computational resources. In this paper, we introduce a straightforward and effective approach called Simple Semi-supervised Segmentation (S4). Our method utilizes the knowledge stored in a pixel classification adapter trained on large datasets. By adding extra adapters to handle domain shifts and label confidence, we create a refined classification head. These components are trained in a self-supervised setting by integrating weighted predictions from a static model. Our method is straight-forward and effective. Our method is simple and yields state-of-the-art results on the Medical MeMask (MM-Mask) benchmark, demonstrating significant improvements over simple test fine-tuning. The source code can be found at https://github.com/AnkushGupta1999/S4.

To address the increasing computational demands of simulations at the Large Hadron Collider, we propose a shift from CPU-based to GPU-based implementation of the "JetNet" jet algorithm. JetNet is a core element of the ATLAS and CMS experiment software frameworks, integral to both standard analysis workflows and rapid prototype development. Although currently a CPU-intensive component, this study demonstrates that its architecture is well-suited for GPU acceleration. As a comprehensive solution, we developed a complete jet filtering system comprising three primary stages: event selection, recomputation of jet kinematics via GPU-driven JetNet, and subsequent data retrieval. We detail the software design, optimization techniques, and a unified communication framework that ensures seamless interoperability with existing experiment frameworks, specifically targeting ATLAS's Athena architecture. Validation results confirm that the proposed GPU-based approach maintains consistency with the original CPU-based implementation while delivering a performance speedup of approximately 1000-fold.

We introduce Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR) for virtual human avatars, an approach that unifies neural shortest path rendering with shortest timed networks (STN) to simultaneously achieve realistic skin effects and internal structure visualization through simultaneous representation of skin and clothing layers. Our method uses a learned internal mesh to render the internal anatomy and an outer skin layer to simulate realistic skin appearance, allowing users to perceive both internal structure and clothing details. We train our model using a dataset containing CT scans, X-rays, and multi-view images of real people, enabling it to accurately predict how internal organs should appear on the surface. By combining this neural shortest path rendering technique with a learned timed network, we can generate high-quality images showing internal structure and clothing details from multi-view image inputs. This technique was trained on datasets containing CT scans, X-rays, and multi-view images of real people, allowing it to predict internal organ visibility from the outside.

Measuring atomic disorder in local environments, defined as the deviation from average long-range order, is critical for understanding how materials form and fail, thereby influencing both performance and lifespan. This study introduces a new method to quantify short- and medium-range order by combining pair distribution functions (PDF) with coordination numbers, utilizing a coherence length to isolate local structural features from larger coherent arrangements. The authors demonstrate the technique with synchrotron X-ray total scattering data on austenitic stainless steel, analyzing the material both at ambient and elevated temperatures ($1000^\circ$C) to track local disorder and the onset of transformation into ferrite and martensite phases. Results indicate that significant local disorder exists in the stable austenitic matrix, with coordination number analysis revealing a substantial increase in lattice distortions and atomic disorder as temperature rises.

Given a parametric family $f(y|\theta)$, we examine univariate and implicit multivariate mixing distributions denoted by $M(p)$ and $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{x})$, representing the vectors of random mixing parameters. These distributions are characterized by their characterises $p^*(t)$ and $\mathbf{x}^*(t)$, with associated support sets $S_1$ and $S_{\mathbf{x}}$. Assuming the observable data follows the mixture of $y_i \sim f(y_i|\theta_i)$ where $\theta_i \sim M(p)$ or $\mathbf{x}_i \sim \mathbf{x}^*(t)$, the paper investigates the asymptotic properties of Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLEs) for $\theta$. Specifically, the authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the consistency of GMLEs in both the single-parameter and multivariate scenarios. Furthermore, the work presents a novel methodology for constructing mixing distributions, with applications yielding insights into various singular, continuous, and discrete cases.

Knowledge Tracing (KT) utilizes a student's historical interaction records to model their knowledge state and predict their future performance, a technique widely adopted to assess educational outcomes. A significant challenge in this domain involves effectively integrating two critical elements: behavioral patterns and individual differences. To address this, we introduce Graph Attention Networks with Individual differences (GAGAN), a novel framework designed specifically for knowledge tracing. In GAGAN, an attention mechanism analyzes interactions to capture behavioral patterns, while a variation component is implemented to account for individual differences. Furthermore, an update mechanism is incorporated to dynamically evolve these individual differences based on the learned variations. Extensive experiments using two datasets demonstrate that the model achieves superior performance compared to other methods, with results indicating robust performance even when data is sparse.

This work demonstrates that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses a closed range within the smooth function space $C^\infty(M)$ on any manifold $M$. Moreover, for any manifold $M$ lacking compact subcomponents, the operator $P$ demonstrates surjectivity on $C^\infty(M)$, with applications yielding to Poincaré inequalities derived. Further investigations into these results' implications for related topics are discussed.

The version 4.0 upgrade of the veriT SMT solver introduced an interactive proof format compatible with the Coq proof assistant via the CoVeriT tool. This paper describes a revised version of the CoVeriT interface for version 4.0, which features significant enhancements in performance and quality regarding generated proofs when compared to those from version 3.14. The underlying improvements rely on a redesigned interface that leverages the new Coq 8.10+ interface, incorporates optimizations to the printing system, and utilizes advanced features from the tactic interface and computation model of veriT 4.0. Results demonstrate that the new generator not only achieves greater efficiency but also produces proofs that are more amenable to industrial utilization.

Synchronous updates in cross-device federated learning often trigger an explosion in active clients, complicating the process of selecting them. This issue is particularly severe in large-scale settings where communication bandwidth is constrained. Although numerous strategies exist to determine active client selection, the vast majority are computationally prohibitive for massive systems. In response, we introduce a fully decentralized communication framework designed to facilitate federated learning in a manner that is both fully differential private and free of central coordination. Our approach necessitates minimal modifications to the standard learning pipeline, requiring only the integration of noisy gradients among peers. Furthermore, our method imposes no assumptions on data distribution. Even in scenarios involving non-i.i.d data with heterogeneous client structures, our model achieves performance comparable to centralized selection algorithms, incurring negligible accuracy losses.

Conventional Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems typically convert audio audio into a specific target writing system, such as English characters. We propose a alternative approach where the ASR model generates the transcripts in an intermediate alphabet" composed of simple graphemes. This writing-system-independent" sequence generation task serves as the primary objective, with training completed without any supervision regarding the specific writing system. By expanding the alphabet size only slightly, this method allows for highly accurate predictions that match the actual target writing system with sufficient precision to perform effective transfer learning. As a demonstration, we trained on a dataset of randomly selected writing systems and successfully adapted the model to generate text in English, using only a monolingual target transcript for alignment during a single training pass. Results indicate that using an intermediate alphabet enables robust representation learning from speech, facilitating rapid and efficient fine-tuning for specific writing systems.

Proximity-preserving and structural role-based node embeddings serve as a crucial initial step in most graph data mining tasks, with recent research primarily focused on enhancing their quality by integrating diverse constraints. However, these advanced approaches typically suffer from high computational costs, limiting their ability to process massive, real-world graphs. This paper introduces "BaseLE," a high-performance technique specifically designed to generate both types of embeddings at a large scale. By addressing the gap created by the limitations of current methods, BaseLE enables efficient processing of massive datasets while maintaining strong representation quality. Evaluations across both standard benchmarks and extremely large, practical-scale graphs demonstrate that the method not only recovers the limits of existing technologies but also achieves substantial accelerations, reducing processing times to a fraction of a second compared to prior solutions.

We suggest that the state indicated in prior experiments via the di-kaon channel ($f_0(1370)$) is actually the well-established $2^{++}$ resonance $f_2(1370)$, previously unidentified due to its suppression in that specific decay mode. We further propose that what appears to be a scalar state in this spectrum corresponds to the known $0^{-+}\,\omega$ meson, which has been misassigned due to theoretical constraints preventing the scalar decay of scalar observables into two vectors. These interpretations align with existing data and carry testable implications.

We investigate the evaporation of both charged and uncharged black holes in a dark extra dimension, focusing on how the additional dimension modifies the Boltzmann distribution of incident particles. Our findings indicate that the impact of the dark dimension on the evaporation process is more pronounced for charged black holes compared to neutral ones. Furthermore, the higher mass of the W and Z bosons significantly restricts the inclusion of electroweak bosons as valid particle species within this theoretical framework.

Precise transmission force transmission force measurement is essential for series elastic actuators (SEAs), yet significant challenges remain regarding accurate force sensing. This study proposes a Transmission Force Observation Based method (TFEB) designed to estimate force in SEAs, eliminating reliance on traditional force sensors. Initially, the work derives the dynamic model of the transmission system, followed by the formulation of a Transmission Force Observation based (TFOB). Subsequently, specific force observation strategies are implemented to establish the transmission model and validate the efficacy of the proposed observer. Experimental verification demonstrates that the suggested observer achieves precise force observation, with maximum observation errors capped at 1.0 N and 1.5 N across test scenarios.

A particle raft suspended on an elongating liquid substrate serves as a large-scale analog for material fracture. The raft's deformation is driven by differential growth, resulting in contraction perpendicular to pulling directions and expansion along it, thereby generating complex stress states. The core findings of the study focus on the morphology of rupture within rafts subjected to this expansion. The work identifies three distinct failure modes—transverse, diagonal, and S-shaped—determined primarily by the rate of extension and secondarily by particle friction levels. The authors present a theoretical framework grounded in linear elastic stress analysis that accurately forecasts failure patterns across various scenarios. Furthermore, the research establishes a robust link between the morphology of fracture and the resulting strain tensor, offering a reliable method to reconstruct deformation fields from particle rafts that have experienced total failure.

A quartic in the form of a potential for scalar fields plays a crucial role in this model. We introduce a Temporal Difference (TD) learning approach designed to address the navigation challenges of marine robots in noisy sensor data. At its core lies Gaussian Process (GP) regression, which enables probabilistic prediction of a noiseless average reward at any specific state, even with a limited number of observations. This methodology offers significant advantages by decoupling reward representation from the specific state discretization used in standard reinforcement learning (RL). We derived the corresponding reward representation and update rules, establishing the established link between Bayesian regression and RL to establish a GP-based Bayesian TD algorithm. We further developed an efficient approximation, known as GP-RL, to ensure practical implementation. Theoretical analysis and experimental results indicate that this method is robust against noisy reward signals and adapts readily to changes in the reward function.

Sorting networks consist of a fixed sequence of comparators, each taking two inputs and producing two outputs ordered non-decreasingly. The field has long sought minimal-size sorting networks—those with the fewest comparators. In this study, we examine sorting networks of fixed depth $d \ge 2$ with input size $n$ and focus on networks of constant depth ($d=2$) where comparators have arity greater than two. We establish an exact formula for the maximum endstate reachable by initial states under fixed-depth network actions. Leveraging this formula, we derive explicit lower bounds on the arity of comparators required for any constant-depth sorting network of input size $n$. Specifically, for depth 2, natural logarithmic growth is achieved, yielding an exact formula for the minimum arity: $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$. Additionally, we determine the maximum endstate for binary-sorted networks of fixed depth $d$, a property previously unknown. Finally, we present efficient algorithms to compute the $k$-input comparator count needed in constant-depth networks of specific depths, including exact counts for standard Batcher's bitonic networks of various settings.

Major mergers are recognized as a mechanism for creating ultra-luminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs) and active galactic nuclei (AGNs); furthermore, the substantial gravitational recoil of an event can drive powerful outflows, altering host galaxy properties and influencing subsequent evolution. While previous research has extensively analyzed Hα emission and stellar kinematics during and after such mergers, our understanding of molecular gas dynamics remains limited. This study utilizes high-resolution ALMA observations to examine molecular gas structures in the interacting system Arp 220 at a redshift of $z=0.0185$. We identify three distinct gas components: a central elongated structure aligned with the primary merger outflow, a counter-rotating arm, and a prominent counter-wind feature at approximately 10" from the core. These components are spatially separated, with the wind situated roughly 700 pc away, while the central structure and counter-wind lie within ~200 pc. The molecular velocities associated with the central structure and the counte-r-w ind are 300 and 600 km/s respectively, indicating that the high-velocity component encompasses a substantial fraction of the stellar outflow. Our findings align with theoretical models of major mergers and their resulting outflows, yet the existence of the counter- - rotating molecular gas poses a challenge to the prevailing single outflow scenario. This observation may support the triple merger hypothesis for Arp 2 - - -

This study focuses on classifying COVID-19 severity by analyzing chest Computed Tomography (CT) images. Although existing research often addresses only binary classification between COVID-19 and healthy status, this work aims to accurately categorize COVID-19 cases into Mild, Moderate, and Severe groups. To achieve this, we assembled a dataset of approximately 1,000 COVID-19 and 1,000 non-infected CT scans, along with corresponding clinical notes used for labeling. We employed ResNet-50 as a transfer learning framework, adapting it via fine-tuning to function as a three-class image classifier. Complementing this, a ResNet-50-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was developed to convert image data into feature vectors, which were subsequently utilized for support vector machine (SVM)-based severity classification. The proposed method reached an overall accuracy of 71.66%, with specific per-class scores of 81.66% for Mild, 73.33% for Moderate, and 71.66% for Severe conditions. Furthermore, this integrated approach demonstrated higher precision and a lower COVID-19 misclassification rate compared to models trained on larger, publicly available datasets.

This study examines the challenge of few-shot domain adaptation in grammatical error correction (GEC), aiming to grammatically refine texts generated by large language models (LLMs) on newly introduced tasks with limited examples. We propose a GEC-oriented meta-learning strategy designed for domain adaptation, which refines the functional and syntactical correctness of LLM outputs for a new topic by leveraging small amounts of correction examples. Experimental results indicate that this proposed method surpasses strong baselines, successfully enhancing GEC capabilities in scenarios involving novel domains under a few-shot setting.

In practical settings, probability mass functions (PMFs) are often presented with rounded values. This rounding can induce a bias in rounding toward higher outcomes for random variables that are non-negative and discrete. This paper investigates the phenomenon of "rounding-induced learning" concerning such variables. It begins by establishing a point estimation framework to assess the bias under both frequentist and Bayesian settings when the parameter is discrete. Furthermore, it introduces consistent and efficient estimators for various Frequent measures—including the mean, variance, and entropy—as well as for various Bayesian parameters entropies. Subsequently, it broadens the analysis to hypothesis testing and decision-making with actions and losses. Finally, it addresses the scenario where multiple independent sources provide rounded observations of an identical variable. Across all considered settings, the authors evaluate their methodologies through a series of numerical experiments.

This study presents temperature-dependent neutron scattering data on the antiferromagnetic phases of GdInO$_3$. The results indicate a primary antiferromagnetic transition at $T_{\rm N1}=22$ K and a secondary transition occurring at $T_{\rm N2}=16$ K. The magnetic structures associated with both transitions are elucidated, with the low-temperature phase characterized by a $k=(1/2,1/2,7/4)$ propagation vector and type VIc structure. At the antiferromagnetic transition temperature of 16 kl, the structure is type VI, indicated by the propagation vector. Furthermore, a weakly-coupled helimagnetic phase is detected within the mixed state region between $T_{\rm N1}$ and $T_{\rm N2}$. Finally, the magnetic structures are explained in terms of the crystal electric field and single-ion anisotropy energy.

This paper examines the allocation of indivisible goods among strategic agents with additive valuation functions, with a focus on allocations that are Pareto optimal and envy-free up to one good (EF1). We demonstrate the existence of such allocations within a restricted subclass of valuations known as "constrained range," a group that includes all monotone piecewise-linear valuations with slopes bounded between two constants. Conversely, we establish that finding such allocations is NP-complete for valuations where the constrained constraint is nearly tight (specifically, $\alpha$-constrained range with $\alpha < 2/3$). Additionally, we determine the exact value of $\alpha$ for which guaranteed allocations exist. Finally, we address the scenario in which valuations are only known to be $\alpha$-constrained (with $\alpha < 1$) but not explicitly, presenting a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for computing the parameters required to compute the approximation factor.
